The Romantic Story of the Mayflower Pilgrims, and Its Place in the Life of To-Day, is by Addison, published at Boston. Addison had also written Old Boston, on its Puritan sons and Pilgrim shrines. Verses by Wordsworth and Mrs Hemans face the title, on farewell and a stern, rock bound coast.

A line from Senator Lodge is quoted at the front. High ideals in the conduct of life are what survive, Lodge said. That is why the Pilgrim narrative stands forth in every history as one of the great events of its time. He spoke at the dedication of the Pilgrim Memorial Monument at Provincetown, on August 5, 1910. A picture shows the Mayflower in Plymouth Harbour, from a painting. Numerous original illustrations go with the text. Readers get the Pilgrim story retold as a living example for modern American life.
3701-letters-from-high-latitudes-being-s:
Lord Dufferin wrote these letters home during a voyage in 1856, when his schooner yacht Foam sailed for Iceland, Jan Mayen, and Spitzbergen. The letters mix high spirits with mishap from the first page, as illness delays the start and a shy Icelandic guide paces the coffee room like a polar bear. Dufferin, later Governor General of Canada and Viceroy of India, writes as a witty young lord seeing the far north for the first time.

Geysers, lava fields, Icelandic balls, and Arctic seas fill the later letters, along with dinners, French savants, and talk of local dress. The book charms because its author laughs at himself as often as he marvels at the sights. Readers who enjoy travel writing with jokes intact will find a fresh account of a north that then felt almost as remote as the moon.
37031-english-and-scottish-ballads-volum:
Francis James Child edits the first volume of a great gathering of English and Scottish ballads, issued at Boston in 1860. Child lists the older collections he drew on and sorts the ballads into books. An old verse at the front promises tales of war and woe, joy and mirth, treachery and fairy folk.

Book one opens with Arthur tales, from The Boy and the Mantle to the marriage of Sir Gawaine and the death of Arthur. Sir Guy, St George and the dragon, and the Seven Champions follow in good order. Thomas the Rhymer, the Young Tamlane, and the Elfin Knight bring in the fairy world. Notes on lines and variants attend each ballad. Readers get the founding texts of ballad study, set out with a scholar's care.
37060-through-these-eyes-the-courageous-:
Through These Eyes, subtitled the courageous struggle to find meaning in a life stressed with cancer, is an autobiography by Lauren Ann Isaacson, whose dates are given as 1961 to 1986. The original hardcover book was copyright 1990, and the text was released into the public domain in 2006.

Front matter gives the Library of Congress card number and the book ISBN. A note from the release explains the text is made freely available to all on the internet. Readers may copy it as often as they like, and send it in total or in part to whomever they wish. Isaacson wrote of her own illness and search for meaning, and the book appeared after her death at twenty five. Readers get a young woman cancer memoir, published posthumously and given freely to the world by her family.
3726-the-decameron-volume-i:
Giovanni Boccaccio wrote the Decameron in the shadow of the Black Death, and this first volume gathers its opening tales. Ten young Florentines, seven women and three men, flee the plague city for a country villa, where they pass ten days telling stories to while away the hours. Each day has a theme, and the tales range from bawdy jokes to high romance, told in turn by each member of the company.

The tales in this volume include lovers parted by violence, a lady whose beauty draws a prince, and rogues who talk their way out of ruin. Boccaccio tells each story with grace and bite, and the frame of gardens, songs, and feasts keeps the plague at a distance. Readers new to the book will find a vivid doorway into medieval Italy, witty, earthy, and humane by turns.
37548-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-88:
Notes and Queries, number 88, is a weekly journal for literary men. It calls itself a medium of inter communication for antiquaries and genealogists. Captain Cuttle's saying fronts it: when found, make a note of. This issue, volume four, is dated Saturday, July 5, 1851. It sold at threepence, or fourpence for the stamped edition then.

Contents open with Our Fourth Volume and the Duke of Monmouth's pocket books. Madden writes that lead note on the rebel duke's papers at length. Folk lore follows: Stanton Drew and its tradition, by David Stevens. Minor notes treat Spencer Perceval and an adventurer in 1632 next. Almanacs, old songs, and word lore crowd the queries that follow.
37845-a-book-of-irish-verse-selected-fro:
A Book of Irish Verse gathers the poems of Ireland's new writers. Yeats, the poet, picked the poems and wrote the first words. The book came out in London in 1900 in a fresh form. It is given to the two groups that kept the land's letters alive.

The run starts with Goldsmith, of the age past, and his old age piece. A priest of a town and a deserter's thoughts stand near the front. Moore's songs of lost days and Wolfe's grave piece are in the list. A felon of Clonmel and an outlaw of a lake sing in their turn. Mangan's dark rose and his keen for dead chiefs close the front run. Notes by the man who picked the poems gloss the work.
38549-the-complete-works-of-richard-cras:
The Complete Works of Richard Crashaw, volume one, gathers the poems of the seventeenth-century devotional poet in the Fuller Worthies Library edition edited by Grosart. Printed for private circulation in 1872, the edition first collated the poems with the early editions and added manuscript poems.

Grosart dedicates the volume to John Henry Newman, in gratitude for spiritual nurture found in Newman's writings, calling Crashaw a poet Newman loves as Englishman and Catholic. The contents open with Steps to the Temple: the Weeper, the Teare, and hymns on the wounds of Christ. A long memorial introduction on Crashaw's life and poetry precedes the poems.
38584-on-the-variation-of-species-with-e:
Wollaston wrote this study of how species vary, published by Van Voorst in London in 1856. Insects stand at the center of his argument, as his title states in full. A couplet from Tennyson, that no compound of this earthly ball is like another, heads the title page as a motto.

An inquiry into the nature of genera follows the main argument in the book. Wollaston sorts beetles and other insects from islands and wild places, weighing how far kinds shade into one another. Three years before Darwin's great book, such careful doubts about fixed species were already in the air among working naturalists.
38776-the-letters-of-henry-james-vol-i:
The Letters of Henry James is a set of the notes of the great tale man, chose and set by Percy Lubbock. The host text is the first part of the set. It was put out at New York in nineteen twenty. The front plate shows the man from a draw by a famed art hand of the year eighteen eighty six. A long lead in and a note stand past the list of parts.

The notes fall in heaps by years. The first heap is the first years past the sea, from eighteen sixty nine to eighteen seventy four. Its notes go to his kin maid, to his dame, to his great kin man of the mind, and to his sire. Notes to a great teach man and to a famed writ man stand in it as well.
39154-special-method-in-the-reading-of-c:
Reading of Complete English Classics in the Common School is a teaching method book by Charles McMurry. Macmillan published the book in 1903 for teachers in the graded common schools. Contents open with the educational value of literature in the school course. The use of masterpieces as wholes, not scraps, heads the second chapter of the work.

Literary materials for the five upper grades are listed and weighed for teachers. Class room method in reading fills the fourth chapter and beyond in the contents. McMurry argues that children should read whole classics, with the teacher guiding the whole. Progressive era educators gain a full plan for literature in the grades.
39199-the-fortunate-isles-life-and-trave:
The Fortunate Isles is a travel book by Mary Stuart Boyd on life and travel in Majorca, Minorca, and Iviza, first printed at London in 1911. Eight colour pictures and fifty-two pen drawings go with the text. Boyd also wrote travel books on a stolen summer and a Versailles Christmas, and novels such as The Glen and The First Stone.

Her forewarning quotes the one Briton they met who had been to the Balearic Islands. He warned them the isles were out of the world, with no tourists, no English spoken, and nothing to do. So we went, Boyd answers. The book opens with the pair leaving London on a stormy mid-October Saturday and walking the Rambla at Barcelona the next night.
39917-narrative-of-an-expedition-to-the-:
The Narrative of an Expedition to the Shores of the Arctic Sea in 1846 and 1847 was written by John Rae, the Hudson's Bay Company surgeon and explorer. Rae led a small party north from York Factory to survey the Arctic coast. His chapters begin with the breaking ice in Hayes and Nelson Rivers, the departure, and slow progress through unbroken fields of ice.

The party reached Churchill, traded with Inuit visitors, and pushed on past inlets, walruses, and reefs toward their survey ground. Rae traveled light and lived off the land, a method that later made his name. His narrative is plain, exact, and observant. It remains a valued record of the Arctic shore and of the peoples who guided and fed the travelers.
40147-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-no-v:
Harpers New Monthly Magazine number six, for November 1850, is part of volume one of the new American monthly. The lead piece is A Pilgrimage to the Cradle of American Liberty, by Benson J Lossing. Lossing tells the tale with both pen and pencil.

Lossing left Boston on a bright October morning to visit Concord and Lexington, towns famed from the first fights for freedom. He rode the Fitchburg rail line, found a guide, and set out to see the old sites. His verse quote at the head comes from Richard H Dana. The piece mixes travel, past, and praise of the land. Readers meet the young magazine in its first year, keen to bind a new nation to its roots.
4055-the-future-of-the-colored-race-in-a:
An article on the future of Black Americans after slavery argues that their condition will overmaster all other questions for years to come. It recalls how the South once sought only to tolerate slavery, then made it the cornerstone of secession, a doctrine former builders had rejected.

The writer weighs what should be done with the freed slave, rejecting hasty plans such as removal by ships, and counting their cost in money and time. The piece speaks from the age of debate over freedom, citizenship, and reunion. Readers gain a direct view of how Americans of that era framed a question that shaped the nation.
40903-motor-boat-boys-on-the-great-lakes:
A boys' adventure novel by Louis Arundel, published at Chicago in 1912. M A Donohue held the copyright. Its subtitle promises exploring the mystic isle of Mackinac. Twenty-three chapters crowd storms, rescues, and the Soo rapids. Josh Purdue and fat Buster are the opening pair. The first chapter puts Buster up a tree.

A bull, not a cow, is pawing the field dirt. Buster's new red sweater suddenly seems a poor choice. Josh, long-legged, runs for the fence at once. Buster sets down his milk bucket and shins up the lone tree. Motor boats take over after the farm comedy. Mackinac Island, wireless day, and a night of anxiety fill the middle. The series rode the new craze for cheap motor boating.
40956-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Eleventh Edition, Volume Fifteen, Slice Five is one bound slice of that great word book of all lore. Its span runs from the head word Joints to the head word Justinian the First. The name page calls the work a book of arts, lore, writ, and broad facts. Notes at the front tell how signs and small marks of the print are kept in this form.

The list of heads in the slice shows its breadth in one glance. Joints take three heads, for flesh, for build craft, and for earth lore. Town heads, bard heads, law heads, and holy book heads crowd the rows. Names of the old east and of the church stand past names of trade towns of the new world. Each head is a full tract by its own hand.
41476-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-134:
Notes and Queries was a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries and genealogists. Volume five, number 134, appeared on Saturday, May 22, 1852, at fourpence. Its motto from Captain Cuttle bids readers make a note of things when found.

Bealby writes a few things about Richard Baxter to lead the notes in this number. Rimbault gives a Latin song by Andrew Boorde, and Shakespeare notes follow in the contents. Halliwell prints manuscript Shakespeare emendations, and Norgate lists publications of the Stuttgart Society, in the small coin of learning the journal passed between its readers each week.
41571-notes-on-the-book-of-deuteronomy-v:
Notes on the Book of Deuteronomy, volume I, is a Bible commentary by C H Mackintosh. Loizeaux Brothers published the American edition at Neptune, New Jersey. The first edition appeared in 1880. This copy is the twenty-seventh printing, dated 1965. A prefatory note from Mackintosh, dated at Scarborough on May 1st, 1879, authorises the Loizeaux edition. Earlier American publishers, he complains, had issued his notes without permission.

The introduction argues that Deuteronomy is no mere repetition of the earlier books. God never repeats Himself, Mackintosh insists, in His Word or His works. Every sentence carries its own distinct meaning and application. The volume then works through the first six chapters at length. Chapter one alone fills more than eighty pages. Mackintosh wrote for readers who held the plenary inspiration of Scripture. His notes mix close reading with direct address to the conscience.
41607-oom-paul-s-people-a-narrative-of-t:
Howard Hillegas wrote Oom Paul's People, printed at New York in 1900, with eight photographs and a map. Oom Paul is President Kruger of the Transvaal. The book tells of the British and Boer troubles in South Africa, with a history of the Boers and their land.

Chapters run from the early Cape settlers and the Great Trek to the Johannesburg gold fields and the Jameson raid. Hillegas sketches Kruger at home, prints a talk with him, and gives Cecil Rhodes a chapter too. Causes of the quarrel, the franchise and suzerainty among them, close the survey.
41979-a-history-of-the-city-of-brooklyn-:
Stephen M Ostrander wrote a history of the city of Brooklyn and Kings County, edited with an intro and notes by Alexander Black. Volume one was issued in Brooklyn by subscription in eighteen ninety four. The run was held to five hundred copies. Ostrander had been a member of the Holland Society and the Long Island Historical Society.

Chapter one treats the land at the time of first finds, its rocks, ice age marks, trees, and beasts. It then treats the native tribes and their fall to the Iroquois. Chapter two takes up Henry Hudson, Dutch aims, and the West India Company. Chapter three weighs Dutch and Puritan ways with the native folk. Local readers will find a close start to the tale of Brooklyn.
42419-the-true-history-of-the-state-pris:
George Agar Ellis wrote The True History of the State Prisoner, Commonly Called the Iron Mask, Extracted from Documents in the French Archives, issued at London in 1826 by John Murray. A French work by J Delort on the man in the iron mask led Ellis to write. Delort had found the prisoner's name in sound state papers, Ellis says.

Ellis faults Delort's part as ill arranged and confused. It is full of fulsome praise of Louis the Fourteenth too, he says. That praise sits ill in a tale of one of that king's most cruel acts, he holds. The theme has great historic curiosity for English readers, he thinks. Ellis throws the tale together in a clearer form from the same archives. The masked prisoner's name and fate are the core of the record.
42460-the-truth-of-christianity-being-an:
The Truth of Christianity examines the chief points of the Christian faith. Its author was Lieutenant Colonel Turton, a layman rather than a clergyman. The hosted text opens with pages of press opinions from earlier editions. Secular papers praised its plain common sense appeal. Church papers called it a storehouse of facts on Christian evidences. Reviewers stressed that Turton holds the scales evenly.

The arguments, they said, are marshalled with logical precision. Difficulties are not evaded but met fairly, one paper noted. A healthy lay atmosphere marks the book's manner. Turton's detached style lets any reader with reasoning power follow him. New editions were thoroughly revised as the book kept selling. The opinions run from 1900 to 1909 across many papers. Few works of popular apologetics won praise from both church and secular press alike.
42725-the-meadow-brook-girls-on-the-tenn:
Janet Aldridge wrote The Meadow-Brook Girls on the Tennis Courts, published by the Saalfield Publishing Company in 1914. Aldridge's series had taken the girls under canvas, across country, afloat, into the hills, and by the sea. This volume sends them to a tournament. Grace Thompson opens the story complaining, in her lisping way, that she wants some excitement. Jane McCarthy answers that the Meadow-Brook Girls never go long without it.

The contents promise tramps guarding a secret, a tramp club, and a discouraging try-out. A steam roller comes to the rescue in the middle chapters. The girls camp on a battlefield, spy out the cup that lures them, and reach the tournament courts at last. Saalfield's series gave girls the camping and sporting adventures that boys' books had monopolised, with tennis as this volume's prize.
42729-stand-fast-craig-royston-volume-i:
William Black issued volume one of his three volume novel Stand Fast, Craig-Royston at London in 1890. Sampson Low published it, and Black's earlier books A Daughter of Heth and Macleod of Dare head the title page. Chapter one, The Wanderers, brings two strangers into sunny Piccadilly on a May afternoon. Fashionable crowds glance at them with care and curiosity.

An old man in a shepherd's tartan plaid walks with a girl of about seventeen. His silver hair and beard frame keen eyes and a firm, cheerful mouth. Her downcast gaze, fine walk, and hair of mixed gold shades mark her at once. Later chapters promise neighbors, fairy land, and an alarm. A Highland tinged romance starts in London.
42930-plotinos-complete-works-v-1-in-chr:
Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie edited Plotinos: Complete Works, with rights held from nineteen eighteen, and this is volume one. Guthrie taught in extension at the University of the South at Sewanee and held degrees from several universities. His plan sets the works of Plotinos in the order they were written, grouped in four periods. A biography by Porphyry opens the volume, with shorter lives by Eunapius and Suidas.

Tables match the old Ennead order to Guthrie's time order and back again. The Amelian books, the first twenty-one works, fill the bulk of this volume. Studies at the end treat the growth of the teaching, its view of matter, and its likeness to Christianity. A full index of subjects, thoughts, and words serves the whole set.
42931-plotinos-complete-works-v-2-in-chr:
Volume Two of the Complete Works of Plotinos, prepared by Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie and issued by the Comparative Literature Press at Alpine, New Jersey, in 1918. The set prints the works in time order, grouped in four periods, with lives of Plotinos by Porphyry, Eunapius, and Suidas, commentary, and studies of sources and influence. This volume covers the Amelio-Porphyrian books, numbers 22 to 33.

The text shown opens the Sixth Ennead's fourth book, on the one identical essence being everywhere entirely present. It asks why the world-soul is everywhere entire in the world-body, and how the soul can have no magnitude yet fill all space. Guthrie adds a full index of subjects, thoughts, and words to the set.
42932-plotinos-complete-works-v-3-in-chr:
Plotinos Complete Works holds the thought of the old Greek sage in English. Kenneth Guthrie set the works in time order and adds lives of the man. The hosted text is the third volume of the four part set. Rights date the work to the year nineteen eighteen.

This book holds works marked thirty four to forty five in that time list. A talk on numbers opens the sixth great book of the sage here. It asks if the many is just the one spread out in space and mind. That spread, it holds, is the root of ill in all that lives. Lives by old hands and word lists frame the dense deep texts.
42933-plotinos-complete-works-v-4-in-chr:
Plotinos Complete Works, volume four, prepared by Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie, was published in 1918 by the Comparative Literature Press at Alpine, New Jersey. Guthrie arranges the works in chronological order, grouped in four periods. A biography by Porphyry, Eunapius, and Suidas stands with them. Commentary, studies in sources and influence, and an index of subjects, thoughts, and words complete the set.

Volume four holds the Eustochian books, forty-six to fifty-four, with commentary. The text opens with the First Ennead, book four, asking whether animals may be termed happy. Living well and happiness, on the Aristotelian view, are practically the same: if living well means following the course of nature without obstacles, singing birds live a life desirable for them. The volume closes Guthrie's four-volume English Plotinos.
4335-the-grounds-of-an-opinion-on-the-po:
The Reverend T. R. Malthus wrote this pamphlet in 1815 as an appendix to his Observations on the Corn Laws of the spring of 1814. In the earlier work he had stated, with strict impartiality, the advantages and disadvantages of restricting the import of foreign corn. Here he gives the grounds of his own opinion on that policy.

Malthus weighs both sides without hiding the case against his view, then argues for the course he thinks safest in Britain's actual circumstances. The pamphlet is a short work of applied economics, written while Parliament debated. It shows Malthus moving from analysis to advice, and it pairs naturally with his 1814 observations.
43421-china-in-america-a-study-in-the-so:
Stewart Culin read a study of the social life of the Chinese in the eastern cities of the United States. He read it before the American Association for the Advancement of Science at New York in 1887, and it was printed at Philadelphia the same year. A map of the province of Kwantung fronts it. The Chinese labourers in America all come from the departments of Kwangchau and Shauking in Kwantung, he begins.

They call themselves Punti, or natives, as against the Hakka, or strangers. They divide into the people of the Sam Yup, the three towns, and the Sz' Yup, the four towns. The tract is little more than a hundred miles square, yet shows much diversity of nature. Culin, an anthropologist, traces how these men lived, worked, worshipped, and kept their customs in eastern cities.
43591-the-life-of-ludwig-van-beethoven-v:
The Life of Ludwig van Beethoven, volume I, presents Alexander Wheelock Thayer's biography in Henry Edward Krehbiel's edition. The Beethoven Association published it in New York in 1921. Krehbiel revised Thayer's English manuscript against the German editions. He concluded the work and translated all documents afresh. A bust of Beethoven by Franz Klein, from 1812, fronts the volume.

The first chapter sets Bonn's world before the birth. Electors of Cologne, from Joseph Clemens to Max Friedrich, rule the scene. Their courts' music and Bonn's operatic repertories are detailed. Christian Gottlob Neefe, the composer's teacher, appears early. Chapter two traces the Belgian ancestors. Grandfather Louis sang tenor at Louvain, then became Bonn's chapelmaster. Father Johann's marriage and character follow. The third chapter reaches the composer's birth, with its conflict of dates. Poverty, a dissipated father, and scant schooling mark the childhood. Neefe's instruction and a Holland visit close the opening movement.
43828-white-wings-a-yachting-romance-vol:
William Black opened his three-volume yachting romance White Wings with Macmillan in London in 1880. Black also wrote The Strange Adventures of a Phaeton and Green Pastures and Piccadilly. He dedicated the tale to Queen Mab, in memory of her first cruise on any yacht.

The record covers a long summer of idleness in 1878. A crowd on a quay watches a great steamer with scarlet funnels round a headland. Mary Avon joins the party, new guests come aboard, and the yacht sails north. Chapters promise plots and counter-plots, a wild studio, and a cry of Dunvegan. Love, sea air, and Highland scenes carry this first volume toward dark tidings.
4390-a-history-of-greek-art-with-an-intr:
F. B. Tarbell wrote this history of Greek art, with an introductory chapter on art in general. The book moves from early Aegean and Geometric work through Archaic sculpture and vase painting to the classical masters and the Hellenistic age. Tarbell explains technique, style, and subject as he goes, for students and general readers.

The history suits readers who want more than pictures: it links temples, statues, and pots to the life that made them. Tarbell writes clearly, with dates and schools kept in order. The volume remains a useful survey of Greek art, from its first experiments to its wide spread across the ancient world.
44578-bentley-s-miscellany-volume-i:
Bentley's Miscellany, volume one, is the first half-yearly volume of Richard Bentley's literary magazine, published in London in 1837. A portrait of George Colman the Younger fronts the volume. The book closes with the editor's address on the completion of the first volume. He borrows the custom of the theatre, where the manager steps forward at the end of a season to thank the audience for past favours.

With unusual candour, the editor confesses that the magazine has been fairly inundated with orders during its six months' campaign. Yet the house places many of the very first authors of the day on its free list. They are invited to write just as much paper as they think proper. A passage preserved in the copy looks ahead: the second volume will open on the first day of July 1837.
44659-secret-service-being-the-happening:
Secret Service is a novel made from William Gillette's famous play, done into book form by Cyrus Townsend Brady. Grosset and Dunlap of New York published it in 1912, and the Kinneys illustrated it. The subtitle promises the happenings of a night in Richmond in the spring of 1865.

Brady dedicates his share of the joint production to the people of the stage. Gillette's play was a landmark of the American theatre, a spy melodrama of the Civil War's last days. Its hero works inside the Confederate capital as the city falls. The novel keeps the play's single night pressure and its telegraph office intrigue. A frontispiece caption quotes the suspicion that a man who wanted to fight would hardly be in an office. Novelizations like this carried stage hits to readers far from any theatre.
44842-three-years-in-western-china-a-nar:
Three Years in Western China tells of three journeys in Szechuan, Kweichow, and Yunnan, by Alexander Hosie of the British consular service in China. A second edition was issued at London in 1897. A picture of the Ichang Gorge, with a salt junk under oars, fronts the book. Hosie writes to show western China as he saw it in 1882, 1883, and 1884.

His preface states that plain aim for the narrative at the start. One chapter was read in part before the Royal Geographical Society. Hosie travelled as a consul, with an eye for trade, rivers, and roads. Salt junks, gorges, and hill towns fill his route in those provinces. Few westerners then knew that vast corner of the empire. The book is a first hand record of its peoples and its traffic.
46114-canada-in-flanders-volume-i:
Sir Max Aitken's Canada in Flanders, volume one, is the official story of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, published by Hodder and Stoughton in 1916. A preface by Bonar Law and an introduction by Prime Minister Borden front the book. Ten editions printed in January and February 1916 alone. Aitken's note confesses the chapters were written under great difficulties and in many moods, and that their excuse is the lively interest in Canada.

He publishes his impressions of the 1st Canadian Division and Princess Patricia's Regiment, from his own observation and from military diaries and official documents. The dedication goes to the officers and men serving, and to the memories of the fallen. Aitken hopes one Canadian woman may draw solace from the record of her dead husband's bravery. The volume carries maps and appendices, and later volumes continued the story.
46191-fighting-without-a-war-an-account-:
Ralph Albertson told of Allied fighting in North Russia after the Great War. Harcourt, Brace and Howe issued Fighting Without a War in New York in 1920. Albertson served as a Y M C A secretary with the army there. Photos from the campaign stand through the book.

He landed at Murmansk just before Thanksgiving of 1918, he writes. Archangel, Shenkursk, and the Vaga column mark his year of service. He left last, sailing September 2 with the final missions and embassies. Readers gain an inside account of a half-hidden war and its costs.
46795-the-pioneer-boys-on-the-great-lake:
The Pioneer Boys on the Great Lakes, or On the Trail of the Iroquois, is Harrison Adams's tale of the border. The Page Company printed it at Boston in 1912, with drawings by Charles Livingston Bull. It stands in the Young Pioneer Series.

The series runs from the Ohio to the Columbia, six volumes in all. A frontispiece shows Kenton in the lead, calling to keep against the rock. The chapters open with an alarm bell and refuge at the blockhouse. A bee tree, a honey thief watched, and a bear hunt follow. Serious news, three French trappers, and Simon Kenton enter in turn. Moccasin tracks that toe in, and Blue Jacket's warning, raise the stakes. The grand hunt, Black Beaver's strike, and the trail of the Iroquois lead to the big water. A bitter disappointment waits at the end.
47351-pilots-of-the-republic-the-romance:
Archer Butler Hulbert wrote on pioneer promoters in the Middle West. A C McClurg and Company issued Pilots of the Republic in Chicago in 1906. Sixteen portraits and drawn initials by Walter J Enright fill the book. The work is given to Charles G Dawes, a modern promoter.

Chapters treat Washington, Henderson, Putnam, Clark, Clay, and Astor in turn. Zeisberger preaching to the Indians at Coshocton fronts the volume. Canals, highways, and land schemes mark the promoters' bold roads west. History readers gain warm lives of the men who staked a young republic's growth.
47722-journal-in-france-in-1845-and-1848:
Thomas William Allies kept this journal in France in 1845 and 1848, with letters from Italy in 1847, and printed it in London in 1849. Allies, rector of Launton, Oxfordshire, subtitled it as concerning the church and education. He dedicates the book to the Church in England, hoping holy examples may stir its people to love and good works.

The journal visits a small seminary at Ivetot, the churches of Rouen, and the seminary of Saint Sulpice in Paris. Contents note catechising, refectory life, the Sisters of Charity, and talks on the Eucharist. Letters and notes record schools, convents, and clergy, as an English churchman weighs French Catholic life at close range.
47847-studies-in-the-theory-of-descent-v:
August Weismann, professor at Freiburg, wrote studies in the theory of descent. Raphael Meldola translated and edited them with notes, and they were published at London in 1882, in two volumes with eight coloured plates. This first volume carries a prefatory notice by Charles Darwin, who commends the author's embryological work and the book before the reader.

Darwin singles out the caterpillars of the sphinx-moths, whose stripes and bright colours once passed for freaks of nature. Weismann shows their colouring a protection, proved in one case by experiment: eye-like spots on a caterpillar's thickened end frightened birds away. Laws of variation and inheritance, and classification by characters at different ages, are the larger stakes.
4801-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
John Lothrop Motley, D.C.L., LL.D., corresponding member of the Institute of France, opens The Rise of the Dutch Republic, A History, dated 1855, with this first volume, its first part of historical introduction. An editor's note introduces the author himself: born in Dorchester, Massachusetts, in 1814, died in 1877, author of the novels Morton's Hope and Merry Mount. Motley served as United States minister to Austria from 1861 to 1867, and to England from 1869 to 1870.

The note adds that Mark Twain mentions his respect for Motley. It quotes Oliver Wendell Holmes, speaking before Boston's city authorities on July 4, 1863, on an observer placed on a national watch-tower in a foreign capital. This volume therefore begins not with the Dutch narrative itself, but with Motley's introduction and the editor's portrait of the historian behind it. Readers starting the history should begin here, before the centuries of feudal background in the second volume's introduction.
4810-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
The tenth volume of Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic covers 1566, part one, dated 1855. Chapter six opens with Francis Junius and his sermon at Culemburg House, then the Compromise, with portraits of Sainte Aldegonde, Louis of Nassau, Toison d'Or, and Charles Mansfeld. A sketch of the Compromise, the attitude of Orange, and his letter to the Duchess follow, with signers of the Compromise and indiscretion of the confederates.

Espionage over Philip by Orange, dissatisfaction of the seigniors, and Egmont's conduct join despair and emigration to England. The Request, a meeting at Breda and Hoogstraaten, and exaggerated statements in the state council follow, with the Duchess's hesitation and an assembly of notables. Debate on the Request and the inquisition, Brederode's character, and arrival of petitioners in Brussels carry the volume on. Readers get Motley's account of the Compromise and the petition of 1566.
4813-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
In 1567, the Dutch revolt against Spanish rule turns sharply against the Calvinist rebels, and John Lothrop Motley follows the crackdown town by town. Government troops crush poorly armed Calvinist forces at Lannoy and Waterlots, while officials press the siege and punish country people who sheltered them.

William of Orange stands at the center of the story. He refuses a new oath demanded by the government, offers to give up all his offices, and works to calm Antwerp during three days of tumult. Readers get a vivid account of a revolt losing its early momentum, and of the prince learning how to lead under pressure.
4815-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Spain answers the Dutch revolt with terror in 1568, and John Lothrop Motley opens this section with the machinery of that repression. The Duke of Alva's Blood Council summons Orange, Count Louis, and others, while the Inquisition proclaims death against the whole population of the Netherlands.

Imprisoned nobles Egmont and Horn face interrogation, formal charges, and pleas over jurisdiction, as their wives, fellow knights, and the emperor press for mercy. Orange replies with a published justification and quietly raises money and troops abroad. The volume captures both the cruelty of the trials and the first plans for armed resistance.
48280-life-movements-in-plants-volume-i:
Life Movements in Plants, volume one, first published in 1918, is Jagadis Chunder Bose's study of how plants answer stimulus. Bose directed the Bose Research Institute and had taught at Presidency College. The volume carries ninety-two illustrations. Its first part treats the response of plant organs.

Bose opens with the tangle of the problem itself. The same stimulus can draw unlike answers from unlike organs. Strength and point of application change the result, as does the tonic state of the tissue. He compares pulvinated organs, which move at a joint, with plain growing organs. His instruments shorten the time of experiment so fine movements can be read like signals.
48742-the-missionary-an-indian-tale-vol-:
Owenson wrote The Missionary, an Indian tale in three volumes, here in a fourth edition from Stockdale of London, 1811. This first volume carries a portrait of the author. The tale is inscribed to the Marchioness of Abercorn.

The first chapter opens not in India but in Portugal, at the start of the 17th century. Portugal, bereft of her own kings, had become a prize fought over by the houses of Braganza, Parma, Savoy, and Medici. Spain's arms settled the quarrel, and Philip the Second's rule pressed the country into a province. Under the cruelties of Olivarez, minister to Philip the Fourth, the spring of national liberty coiled tighter. Portugal split into two factions, Spanish partisans and Portuguese patriots. Out of that divided kingdom the missionary of the title must sail for India. Romance readers get the East approached through a fallen empire's politics.
49245-the-unexploited-west-a-compilation:
The Unexploited West, printed at Ottawa in 1914 under Lynch of the Railway Lands Branch, sets out the resources of northern Canada west of Hudson Bay. Its compiler, Ernest Chambers of the Corps of Guides, gathered the facts for settlers and officials under Roche, Minister of the Interior. He signs himself Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod.

Chambers writes that newcomers are using up the Fertile Belt. Settlement now spills north of the North Saskatchewan and into the Peace River valley, and the old picture of the north as a frost-bound waste is fading. Fur traders, explorers, missionaries, geologists and sportsmen supply the reports on soil, timber, rivers, minerals, fish and game that fill the volume.
49634-attila-a-romance-vol-i:
James wrote this romance of Attila in two volumes, published by Harper at New York in 1838. James dedicates the book to Walter Savage Landor as a testimony of regard and admiration. Readers may expect something of the Princess Honoria here, his advertisement begins by warning.

They will find nothing of her, he says plainly at the front. All that is known of her history is uninteresting, and her character disgusting to lovers of purity, he argues. James turns instead to Attila and his Huns, building courts, camps and battles from the scant record of Rome's last century in the west.
49990-women-in-english-life-from-medi-va:
Georgiana Hill wrote Women in English Life, a two-volume work issued at London in eighteen ninety-six. Hill had earlier written a history of English dress. This first volume carries a portrait of Lady Fanshawe at its front.

Hill aims to show the place women have held in national life since Saxon times. She stresses the phases that best show change, under forces like the Church and feudal rule. Names serve as examples, not as full lives. Home life gets the most room, since it concerns the most women. Letters and art are noted in brief, as marks of social advance through the ages.
50191-mrs-beeton-s-dictionary-of-every-d:
Mrs Beeton's recipes stand in letter order in a dictionary of every-day cookery issued in London. The book was the first of a set of practical manuals called the All About It books. Its price of three shillings and sixpence sat between her large household work and her shilling cookery book.

The preface says every recipe keeps the plain plan of her larger work, with warnings on what not to do set beside directions. Cross references are cut to a few by a clear system of arrangement. Almond cake opens the dictionary, with blanched almonds pounded to paste and eggs divided for beating. Small points get the same care as hard ones, since trifles make perfection, the preface insists. Home cooks get a full kitchen reference in quick-lookup form.
50350-history-manners-and-customs-of-the:
History, Manners, and Customs of the Indian Nations is a work by John Heckewelder of Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. The Historical Society of Pennsylvania published this new and revised edition in 1881. Its full title names the nations who once inhabited Pennsylvania and the neighbouring states. William Reichel supplied an introduction and notes. The society's publication fund had issued nine volumes by then. A portrait of Heckewelder fronts the book.

Heckewelder had lived among the peoples he describes. His account preserves their traditions, government, and daily ways. The society's trustees held twenty three thousand dollars for such publishing. Life subscribers paid twenty five dollars for all its books. The editors alone answer for opinions in the volumes, the notice says. Heckewelder's history remains a primary source for the Lenape and their neighbours.
50866-the-life-and-reign-of-edward-i:
The Life and Reign of Edward the First was written by the author of The Greatest of the Plantagenets, whose name the title page withholds. Seeley, Jackson and Halliday of Fleet Street, London, published the book in 1872. A frontispiece shows Edward after an engraving by Vertue, taken from the statue at Carnarvon Castle.

In the preface the author explains that the earlier volume was only an historical sketch, compiled among the manuscripts of the British Museum in one spring and summer. Its reception far exceeded his hopes. Many readers who granted the general truth of the narrative still charged him with partisanship and a one-sided view. He answers that such a task, explaining causes and leading minds to what he deemed the truth, could hardly be done without giving objectors that opening. The book argues its case for Edward openly.
51142-the-times-red-cross-story-book-by-:
The Times Red Cross Story Book gathers stories by famous novelists serving in His Majesty's forces, published by Hodder and Stoughton for the Times fund for the sick and wounded. Every contributor is identified by his regiment. The names include Mason of the Manchester Regiment, Milne of the Royal Warwickshires, Compton Mackenzie of the Royal Navy and Quiller-Couch of the Cornwall Light Infantry.

The first story, Mason's Dimoussi and the Pistol, opens in Morocco. South of Mequinez stretches a tract of uncharted country, lawless and forbidden, which even the great fighting Sultan omitted from his expeditions. There, at Agurai, the boy Dimoussi was born, called the Englishman though he looked an Arab with a strain of Negro blood. The volume is wartime charity publishing at its most star-studded: literature enlisted, quite literally, for the hospitals.
51308-my-strange-rescue-and-other-storie:
My Strange Rescue and Other Stories of Sport and Adventure in Canada is a book of tales by Oxley. His past books of the wild west coast and of the ice seas are named past his name. It was put out in nineteen hundred and three in three towns of two lands. A first note at the front gives his thanks. Those thanks go to the lords of the sheets in which most of these tales first ran.

The sheets named in that note are sheets for the young of two lands. The list of parts is a roll of the north wilds. My most strange save heads the run. A bless in a stern garb, in risk at a black run, and touch and go come next.
51326-the-principles-of-chemistry-volume:
Mendeléeff wrote The Principles of Chemistry, here in its first volume of two. George Kamensky translated it from the sixth Russian edition, and Lawson edited the English text. Longmans printed it at London in 1897.

The translators' preface says Mendeléeff spent his life bringing the scattered facts of chemistry within the domain of law. His teaching presses the principles of the science, the broad rules under which facts group themselves. Of those rules the periodic law ranks first since the atomic theory. Mendeléeff, the preface notes, was led to find it while preparing the first Russian edition of this very book.
51944-a-gray-eye-or-so-in-three-volumes-:
Frank Frankfort Moore's novel opens its first volume with talk in a boat on an Irish hillside. Hutchinson and Company issued the sixth edition from Paternoster Row, London, in 1893, and Moore's earlier books include I Forbid the Banns and Dalreen.

Harold and Edmund debate woman in the abstract while Brian, the third man, makes a show of rowing. Edmund lays down his rule: praise of Woman means the woman one loves, and blame of her means the woman who will not love. Brian breaks in with the tale of Larry O'Leary, the wary potheen maker who rolled keg after keg down Slieve Gorm. The Excise once offered five pounds for word of a private still, yet Larry stayed ahead of the police for years.
52132-sunshine-and-storm-in-rhodesia-bei:
Sunshine and Storm in Rhodesia, by Frederick Courteney Selous, was printed at London in 1896, with a map and many plates. Its full line states the arc: events in Matabeleland before and in the late native revolt, up to the end of the Bulawayo Field Force. Selous first shows a calm farm life at Essexvale: trees set out, game thick by the river, and fair ties with the local folk. Then hints of storm crowd in.

Word of Jameson's fall, a seer's dark claim, and the cattle plague shake the peace. A native cop is slain, herds are swept off, and whole white homes are wiped out in the first raids. Selous takes his wife to Bulawayo and rides back with a small horse force. War fans get a famed hunter's own grim record of the rising.
53627-the-bread-and-biscuit-baker-s-and-:
The Bread and Biscuit Baker's and Sugar-Boiler's Assistant is a trade manual by Robert Wells. Crosby Lockwood published this second edition at London in 1890. Wells was a working baker, confectioner, and pastrycook of Scarborough. Recipes fill the book: bread, tea cakes, hard and fancy biscuits. Buns, gingerbreads, shortbreads, and pastry follow in their sections. Custards, fruit cakes, confections, lozenges, and ice creams widen the range.

Remarks on the art of bread making accompany the recipes. A chapter applies chemistry to bread making as well. The preface offers the book to learners and to daily shop use. Every recipe, Wells says, was tested by actual successful use. A second edition was needed within months of the first. Sections and a full index make the little book a bakehouse reference. Wells wrote from the trade, for the trade.
53775-a-bible-school-manual-studies-in-t:
A Bible School Manual: Studies in the Book of Revelation, by Stephen Alexander Hunter, was published by the Pittsburgh Printing Company at Pittsburgh in 1921. The manual gives an introduction, analysis, and notes, with a concise interpretation according to the symbolic view and general mention of other interpretations.

The text of Revelation is the American Revised Version, edited in paragraphs, used by permission of Thomas Nelson and Sons. Hunter, writing from the Western Theological Seminary at Pittsburgh, dedicates the volume to his classmates and fellow pilgrims. A map of proconsular Asia, following Ramsay, accompanies the study.
54010-the-younger-sister-a-novel-vol-i:
Mrs Hubback wrote The Younger Sister, a novel in three volumes, of which this is the first. Thomas Cautley Newby published it at London in 1850. She dedicated the work to the memory of her aunt, the late Jane Austen. She was taught from childhood to esteem her aunt's virtues and admire her talents. The tale opens with the Reverend John Watson of Winston. He held the living for twenty years.

Watson was once a husband and the father of five children, with a sixth soon added. While his wife lived, her good judgment kept his standing in the parish. With her life, his energy departed. He sank into indolence and fancied ill-health. His children grew up motherless and unchecked. Hubback builds her story on the Watson household, in her aunt's world of country parishes and small incomes.
54500-journal-of-a-west-india-proprietor:
Matthew Gregory Lewis wrote Journal of a West India Proprietor. John Murray issued it at London in 1834. Lewis wrote The Monk and Tales of Wonder. Byron wished him alive again in a motto line. The journals came from his own hand papers. He died at sea on the voyage home in 1818.

Two stays in Jamaica fill the book, 1815-16 and 1817. The journal opens with a wait to sail. Gravesend's noise, dirt, and dullness vex him there. A dingy sky hangs over the river, he writes. November 8, 1815 marks his leaving London. A planter's day book from the last years of British slavery, the journal shows estate life in a voice both witty and blind to much around it.
54646-a-supplementary-report-on-the-resu:
Edwin Chadwick wrote a state report on burial in towns and its harms. The report came out in London in 1843. It was shown to both Houses of Parliament by royal word. Chadwick was a barrister asked by the Home Secretary to probe. His main brief dealt with the health of the work folk of Britain.

Town grave yards stood full in the midst of homes, he found. He weighs claims that corpse air does no harm at all. His facts link foul air from the dead to sharp disease. He asks that town burial end and new grounds be set apart. Health past fans get a grim, key brief. The facts are set out point by point.
54662-a-defence-of-the-inquiry-into-mesm:
A Defence of the Inquiry into Mesmerism and Phrenology, chiefly in relation to recent events in Lynn, by William Armes, was published at Lynn in 1843. Armes offers his address to the candid and sober minded among his fellow townsmen. He says he is guided by no wish to prop up a new and possibly false theory.

Nor, he says, does he wish to cry down, without study, any science however adverse to his prior ideas. Mesmerism and mesmeric phrenology had long held the town attention. The shows called forth credulous wonder in one class, unworthy ridicule in another, and patient, quiet study in a third. Two pamphlets on the subject had already appeared. Readers get a town defence of a strange new science, written at the height of its fame.
55619-the-theory-of-environment-an-outli:
The Theory of Environment, by Armin Hajman Koller, was a doctoral thesis sent to the University of Chicago and printed in 1918. Koller taught German at the University of Illinois. Part one traces the past of the idea of milieu and its state in his day.

Koller starts with what the French word milieu means, from its root sense of a mid place. He then sketches the idea from old times to the start of the 1800s, and on through that age. Parts treat land, place, and past, and how soil and scene shape peoples. A quote from Robert Browning stands at the front. Scholars of thought and letters will find a neat map of how one key idea grew and spread.
55844-military-service-and-adventures-in:
A cavalry officer tells his wars in Military Service and Adventures in the Far East, volume 1 of 2, printed in London in 1847. No name is given. The book holds sketches of the campaigns against the Afghans in 1839 and the Sikhs in 1845 and 1846.

He gives the set to Henry Lushington, with plain thanks and no flattery. Heads take him to India and the north west provinces, then to the Himalayah hills. He marches through Delhi to Ferozepore and meets Runjeet. Past the Indus and through the Bolan Pass he rides to Kandahar. The storm and capture of Ghuzni crown the run, as Dost Mahomed flees his host.
5652-thoughts-out-of-season-part-i:
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote Thoughts Out of Season, part one, in the first complete and authorized English translation edited by Oscar Levy, translated by Anthony M. Ludovici. This first volume pairs two early essays: David Strauss, the Confessor and the Writer, and Richard Wagner in Bayreuth. An editorial note and a translator's preface frame the essays.

The Strauss essay attacks a fashionable German thinker, while the Wagner essay celebrates the composer at Bayreuth as a cultural hope. Readers get Nietzsche young, polemical, and passionate, before his later aphoristic books. It suits anyone tracing how his philosophy began.
57350-military-service-and-adventures-in:
Military Service and Adventures in the Far East, volume two, is the memoir of a British cavalry officer who served in India. The writer names no name on the title page. The book was published in London in 1847, in two volumes.

The volume opens with the rising across Afghanistan and the defence of Jellalabad, then follows General Pollock's advance on Kabul. A ride across central India to Bombay and a posting to Meerut follow. The heart of the book is the war against the Sikhs in 1845 and 1846. Chapters treat the Sikh army, the crossing of the Sutlej, and the battles of Moodkee and Ferozeshuhur. The fighting at Aliwal, where Sir Harry Smith beat the Sikhs and drove them across the river, comes later in the campaign.
57480-four-years-in-the-underbrush-adven:
Four Years in the Underbrush is an anonymous account of adventures as a working woman in New York. Scribner's published it in 1921. The author dedicates it to Sister Wee Wee and dates her dedication from Tampa, Florida, in March 1921. The first chapter is headed For Polly.

The writer spent four years in the city's underbrush of cheap rooms, jobs, and hunger. She worked at trades open to women and wrote down what the life did to those inside it. The book belongs to the literature of disguised investigation, in which a writer of means lives the poor life to report it. Its plain record covers landladies, factories, and the search for the next meal.
57678-elements-of-criticism-volume-i:
Volume one of the Elements of Criticism, in three volumes, was printed at Edinburgh for A Millar of London and A Kincaid and J Bell of Edinburgh. The volume opens with a dedication to the King, urging that the fine arts have ever been encouraged by wise princes for their beneficial influence in society.

The dedication argues that fine arts unite different ranks in the same elegant pleasures, promote benevolence, cherish love of order, and inspire delicacy of feeling. The work itself treats of the fine arts. It attempts to form a standard of taste by unfolding the principles that ought to govern every individual's taste. Its author laments that refining taste is scarce endeavoured in any seminary of learning, though taste is early susceptible of culture and hard to reform once perverted.
593-a-selection-from-the-writings-of-guy:
Guy de Maupassant's short stories of tragedy and comedy fill this first of three volumes, with a critical preface by Paul Bourget. Mademoiselle Fifi, The Horla, Miss Harriet, The False Gems, Simon's Papa, and A Country Excursion lead the set of twenty-seven tales. Bourget praises Maupassant's swift rise and his art of hiding himself in his work.

Maupassant writes with cold, precise prose, where a twist or a single detail unmasks pride, greed, or lust. Normandy peasants, Paris clerks, and soldiers share the stage. The volume serves as a fine entry to a master of the short tale, where life's comedy turns, in a line, to tragedy.
5997-maximilian-in-mexico-a-woman-s-remi:
Sara Yorke Stevenson recalls the French intervention in Mexico from 1862 to 1867, and the reign of Maximilian. Her volume grew from five Century Magazine articles, which Matías Romero, Mexico's minister to Washington, urged her to publish in more lasting form. She dedicates the book to his memory.

The contents run from the Triple Alliance and the Napoleonic idea through Puebla, the allies' rupture, and the French advance. They close with a cloud no bigger than a man's hand, the end of the intervention, and Maximilian's black decree of October 1865. Stevenson writes as a witness to a doomed empire.
60260-the-five-nations-volume-i:
The Five Nations, Volume One, is a book of poems by Rudyard Kipling. It is part of the Service Edition of his works, printed by Methuen of London. The book first came out in September 1903 and went through many editions in the years that followed. The fifteenth edition of 1914 was the first in two volumes. This is the first of those two. A long dedication poem stands at the front of the book.

That dedication speaks of storms that break at midnight and of floods that rise against the land. Kipling had made his name with tales and verse of India and of soldiers. Here the verse turns to the five nations of the empire and to the price of holding them together. The volume is the first half of one of his best known books of poems.
60696-the-boy-travellers-in-australasia-:
Thomas W Knox wrote The Boy Travellers in Australasia, published by Harper and Brothers at New York in 1889. The book gives the adventures of two youths in a journey to the Pacific islands and through the Australian colonies. The Sandwich, Marquesas, Society, Samoan, and Feejee islands stand in the title. New Zealand, New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria, Tasmania, and South Australia complete the circuit.

Knox had written the Far East set in five volumes, each complete in itself. Japan and China, Siam and Java, Ceylon and India filled the first three. Egypt and Palestine and Africa closed that set. South America, the Russian Empire, and the Congo got volumes of their own at three dollars each. The Australasia volume extends the same plan south. Knox's travellers taught geography by itinerary to American boys for a generation.
60880-alice-grand-duchess-of-hesse-princ:
Alice, Grand Duchess of Hesse is a biographical sketch and letters of Princess Alice, second daughter of Queen Victoria. Putnam published it in New York and London in 1885. A portrait of Alice in 1878 fronts the book. Princess Christian, her sister, wrote the preface. The contents divide her life by years, from childhood in 1843 to the end in 1878.

Sections treat her girlhood, her new home at Darmstadt, and her years at work. Trials fill the years 1873 to 1877. An appendix holds a sketch in memoriam by Theodore Martin, dated the day she died. Alice died of diphtheria after nursing her own children through it, and the book is her family's memorial.
6151-athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-i:
Edward Bulwer Lytton dedicates Athens: Its Rise and Fall, book one, to Henry Fynes Clinton. Clinton wrote the Fasti Hellenici, and Lytton thanks him for help drawn throughout his labors from that memorable work.

Lytton argues that chronology is not a dry pile of barren dates. For readers seeking true links between causes and effects, it is the explanation of events and the philosophy of facts. Clinton's Fasti throws light where chronology best repairs deficiency and elucidates obscurity in scanty authorities. This book alone is described here. Clinton's Fasti guides Lytton's dates throughout.
61901-the-mythology-of-greece-and-rome-w:
The Mythology of Greece and Rome, with Special Reference to Its Use in Art, is a manual edited by Bianchi. Chapman and Hall of London issued this revised edition, with sixty-four illustrations.

The preface says a clear, readable account of the legends in moderate compass was long wanted. Dictionaries of mythology, it argues, give no view of the subject as a whole. Costlier works could not serve as class-books. The publishers therefore brought the book out in an English dress. As for present use, the preface points to the galleries and museums. Their works of art need Greek and Roman myth for full appreciation. European literature is coloured throughout by these legends, and poets still draw on them.
62396-parodies-of-the-works-of-english-a:
Parodies of the Works of English and American Authors, volume one, is a set of jest forms with notes by Walter Hamilton. It came out at London in eighteen eighty-four. Hamilton was a man of two lore guilds and wrote past books on song and stage. This book holds jest forms of the verse of five named bards of two lands.

A front quote holds that jest form strikes but at what is false in a work, as a kind of keen note in jest dress. Hamilton first meant to print but a few of the best jest forms of each hand. The first prints sold so fast that the set was made as full as it could be. Loans of rare books and of jest forms from those who bought in made that growth real.
62618-selected-essays-of-plutarch-vol-i:
T G Tucker chose and turned into English essays of Plutarch, here Volume One. The Clarendon Press issued the set at Oxford in 1913. Tucker taught classical philology at the University of Melbourne. A long front essay sets Plutarch in his age of keen, practical letters.

Pieces treat flatterers and friends, advice to married pairs, and the dinner of the seven sages. Garrulity, busybody ways, and old men in public life fill the set. Tucker likens Plutarch to a Greek Addison, full of ideas for daily conduct. Students gain wise, readable moral essays in a fine, clear form.
62981-a-history-of-the-trials-and-hardsh:
A History of the Trials and Hardships of the Twenty-Fourth Indiana Volunteer Infantry is a regimental history printed at Indianapolis in 1913. Its author, Richard J Fulfer, says in the preface that the history rests on the pocket memorandum he kept during the Civil War, from 1861 to 1865. Portraits of Fulfer and of the regiment's colonel head the book.

The front matter lists the corps commanders under whom the regiment served: Fremont, Grant, Banks, Canby, and Sherman. Division officers named include Pope, Lew Wallace, and Hovey. The regiment's own officers and the officers of Company A are listed name by name, down to the corporals and the musician. Such rolls fill many pages of these veterans' histories. The book preserves one regiment's service in the western war. It is the record of common soldiers, kept by one of their own from notes made at the time.
63358-memoir-of-roger-williams-the-found:
James Knowles published his Memoir of Roger Williams with Lincoln, Edmands at Boston in 1834. Knowles taught pastoral duties at the Newton Theological Institution in those years. A facsimile of Williams's handwriting, copied from a paper of 1677, fronts the book. Governor Hopkins supplies the motto, praising Williams as the first modern lawgiver of conscience.

Rhode Island citizens receive the dedication of the volume with respect from its author. The preface teases Americans for dreaming of future glory over past deeds. Youthful nations, Knowles argues, spring forward while old ones look back in longing. Williams, founder of Rhode Island, stands against that tide as a man to remember. Liberty of conscience anchors the life from its first pages.
63588-within-the-pale-the-true-story-of-:
Within the Pale, the true story of anti-Semitic persecution in Russia, by Michael Davitt, was published in a special edition at Philadelphia in 1903. Davitt wrote Leaves from a Prison Diary and The Boer Fight for Freedom. Part one tells the story of the Russian Jew from old times to the Kishineff massacres. Part two gives the massacres in grim detail.

Chapters treat the Pale of Settlement from 1804 to 1882, the Ignatieff laws, and a murder-making legend. Added pages print a list of the killed, reports by two Christian ladies, and letters from Tolstoy and Gorky, with Roosevelt on the crime. Davitt writes as a witness for the defense of a wronged people, with documents to back his plea.
63598-the-essentials-of-logic-being-ten-:
Bernard Bosanquet, formerly fellow of University College, Oxford, published these ten lectures on judgment and inference with Macmillan in 1895 under the title The Essentials of Logic.

The contents open with the problem of logic and the world as idea, then define judgment as the consciousness of a world. Later lectures treat the relation of logic to knowledge, types of judgment, and the proposition and the name. Denotation and connotation get their own sections, as do the parts of the judgment and its unity. The categorical and hypothetical judgments follow in lecture seven. Bosanquet argues that knowledge itself takes the form of judgment, necessary, universal, and constructive. Philosophy students get the Oxford idealist's logic course between covers.
64354-me-myself-and-i:
Kenneth Putnam wrote a time travel tale first printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1947. Professor Ruddle has built a time machine and needs a man to ride it. His pick is Gooseneck McCarthy, a drifter who came to his North Carolina shack in want of food. The price for the trip is one hundred dollars.

Ruddle warns that one slip could wreck the time stream for all. McCarthy, calm and slow to care, must go back one hundred and ten million years. No human kin lived in that deep past. The clash of a cool drifter and a tense scholar drives the fun and the risk.
64434-a-pictorial-atlas-of-fossil-remain:
Pictorial Atlas of Fossil Remains is a plate book of fossils with descriptions by Gideon Mantell. Its coloured illustrations are selected from two earlier works on old life. They are Parkinson Organic Remains of a Former World and Artis Antediluvian Phytology. 

The frontispiece shows the perfect series of bones of the right foot of the moa, the extinct giant bird of New Zealand. The bones were found embedded in an erect position in a deposit at Waikouaiti by Walter Mantell. The bird itself stood about ten feet high, the plate notes say. Figures show the under surface of its first, second, and third toes at a third of natural size. Plate books like this one carried the new science of fossils to readers who could not visit a museum, in the decades when the word dinosaur was still young.
64464-salve-venetia-gleanings-from-venet:
Salve Venetia gathers gleanings from Venetian history by Francis Marion Crawford. Macmillan published the two volumes in 1906. Joseph Pennell supplied 225 illustrations. This first volume runs from the beginnings to the fifteenth century. A list of the doges closes the history.

The chapters open with the little golden age. They pass to the republic of Saint Mark. Early doge families fill several chapters. Venice and the first crusades come next. A chapter treats Venice and Constantinople. Manners and customs of the fourteenth century get a chapter of their own. The conspiracy of Marino Faliero follows. The war of Chioggia ends the main tale. Crawford calls Venice the most personal of all cities.
64777-he-that-will-not-when-he-may-vol-i:
Oliphant opened a three volume novel, published by Macmillan in 1880, at a great house called Markham Chase. Easter is ending, and the fine guests have melted away to town. Sir William Markham, once a minister for the colonies and once head of the Board of Trade, is also gone. He is away settling the plans of his party with its chief.

His absence, the teller says, is no relief, for the family admire him greatly. Yet once he and the guests are gone, the house slides into a happy nursery life. Lady Markham leads the fun herself. There are picnic teas in the woods. Two schoolboys and two little girls rule the house, and even old Nurse dare not scold. The title warns that a chance let slip may not come again, and the tale turns on such a chance.
64953-the-follies-of-a-day-or-the-marria:
Thomas Holcroft translated Beaumarchais's comedy The Marriage of Figaro, printed at London in 1785 under the title The Follies of a Day. The text follows the play as it was then performing at the Theatre-Royal in Covent Garden. Holcroft, author of the comedy Duplicity and the opera The Noble Peasant, signs an advertisement thanking the public for past, present, and future favors.

In that address he is careful to give the chief credit where it belongs, saying the principal excellencies of the play are another man's right and that claiming them would be ridiculous. The edition keeps the original stage directions, marks with inverted commas the passages omitted in the Covent Garden performance, and prints the old long s as the modern letter. A list of the dramatis personae shows which lines actors were expected to leave out.
65008-u-s-marine-operations-in-korea-195:
United States Marine Operations in Korea, 1950 to 1953, volume two, The Inchon-Seoul Operation, was issued in 1955 by the Historical Branch at Headquarters Marine Corps, Washington. Lynn Montross and Captain Nicholas Canzona of the Marine Corps wrote it. Signatures of the Commandant, General Shepherd, and of the assistant chief of staff stand at the front.

The first chapters build the landing: the Communist challenge, the call for a Marine division, and the minute men of 1950 as the reserve poured into Camp Pendleton. Operation Plan Chromite follows, with MacArthur in conference and the scheme of maneuver set. Then the assault: Green Beach, Red Beach under fire, Cemetery Hill, Kimpo airfield, and the push to the beachhead line.
65478-philosophumena-or-the-refutation-o:
Philosophumena, or the Refutation of All Heresies, volume one, turns a Greek work of Hippolytus into English. F Legge made the version from the text of Cruice, and it came out in London in 1921. Hippolytus, bishop and martyr, wrote in about the year 220. The work was long laid to Origen by error.

A long essay tells how the lost books were found, and who wrote them. Book one sums up the Greek wise men, from Thales to the Stoics. Book four bares the tricks of star gazers and magi. Book five starts on snake cult sects and their strange creeds. Church scholars get a prime source on early sects, in a tale of loss and find as rich as a romance.
65631-may-vol-i:
May, volume one, by Mrs Oliphant, is a novel of a Scottish family. Tauchnitz issued it at Leipzig in 1873 for continental readers in English. Volume thirteen twenty three of the British Authors collection holds this copy. The book is inscribed to the golf club of Saint Andrews members.

The Hay Heriot house of Pitcomlie opens the tale, old but not great. Centuries there brought no great men and no great rogues to the line. Lairds stayed steady; younger sons spent the family wildness abroad instead. One younger son went out in the forty five rising, harmlessly for the house. Indian curiosities and trophies from those stray sons enriched the hall.
6606-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Charles Skinner opens his American lore set on the Hudson and its hills, where Rip Van Winkle sleeps, Catskill gnomes play, and a witch works her will. The volume lists tales from Pokepsie to Niagara, with a galloping Hessian, a storm ship, and a trapper's grim revenge among them. Each short tale ties a place name to a ghost, a trick, or a warning.

Skinner retells these stories in plain, brisk prose, as if heard from a neighbor who knows the river well. The Hudson volume sets the tone for the whole set: local, eerie, and fond of a twist. Readers who like place-based ghost lore will find this first book a lively start.
66168-notes-and-queries-number-202-septe:
Notes and Queries number 202, for Saturday, September 10, 1853, is one issue of the London weekly for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. One copy cost fourpence. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, is when found, make a note of.

The notes hold pieces on Milton and Malatesti, a tale of that Swinney, and Tom, mythic and material. Shakespeare correspondence from T J Buckton and Thomas Keightley follows. Minor notes treat a Gray line on the ploughman, poetical tavern signs, and a spurious edition of Baily Annuities. Queries ask on Samuel Wilson, the Rothwell family, the definition of a proverb, and a Latin riddle. Replies to minor queries close the issue. Scholars of the day traded facts and puzzles in these dense pages.
66342-south-africa-vol-i:
Anthony Trollope travelled to South Africa in 1877 and published his account in two volumes, this fourth edition dated 1878. Volume one opens with early Dutch history and English history, then population and federation, before turning to the Cape Colony town by town.

Chapters cover Capetown and its legislature, Knysna, the Cango Caves, the Paarl, and Grahamstown, then British Kafraria and Kafir schools. The volume closes with Natal, its history and condition, the Zulus, and the case of Langalibalele. Readers get a famous novelist working as a travelling reporter, judging colonies, scenery, and native policy with a brisk Victorian confidence.
67669-a-marriage-in-high-life-volume-i:
A Marriage in High Life, volume one of two, is a novel edited by the authoress of Flirtation. Henry Colburn printed it at London in 1828. Her preface warns that the pages may not attract general interest. They hold passages in the history of one heart, placed in singular and trying circumstances.

Readers who knew the real woman, she hints, will recognize her under the feigned name of Lady Fitzhenry. The tale opens with a wedding by special license in Harley Street. Emmeline Benson marries Ernest, Lord Fitzhenry, only son of the Earl of Arlingford, about the middle of August. Her father, a rich city merchant and banker, wears a coat whose first gloss is not yet off. The marriage joins new money to an old title.
68142-from-north-pole-to-equator-studies:
From North Pole to Equator gathers studies of wild life in many lands by Alfred Brehm. Thomson translated the papers from the German, and another Thomson edited them. Blackie published the English volume in London in eighteen ninety six. Eighty three pictures from the author's own drawings fill its pages.

Brehm first gave these studies as public lectures to German audiences at home. HisTierleben and Bird Life had made him Germany's great teller of animal life. The bird bergs of Lapland open the tour, with eider ducks and razor bills. The tundra and its foxes, lemmings, and reindeer follow in the next paper. Asiatic steppes, Siberian forests, and their game fill the middle of the book. The editor adds an essay on Brehm's place among traveller naturalists.
68291-studying-the-short-story-sixteen-s:
Studying the Short-Story, by Berg Esenwein, pairs sixteen classic tales with a study method for schools. Hinds, Hayden and Eldredge issued the revised edition in New York, with copyrights of 1912 and 1918. Esenwein edited The Writer's Monthly and a whole library for writers.

The tales are sorted into four kinds, each with an essay on its author. Stories of action hold Mérimée's Mateo Falcone and a Stevenson night tale. Mystery and fantasy pair Poe's Purloined Letter with the Monkey's Paw by Jacobs. Emotion brings Daudet's Last Class and a Kipling tale of India. Study questions follow each group, with lists of ten more tales of the same kind. The plan lets a class read, judge, and then try the craft itself.
68805-water-and-power-for-san-francisco-:
Water and Power for San Francisco from Hetch-Hetchy Valley is an argument by Martin Vilas. Vilas held bar membership in California, Vermont, and Washington state. He took the rights himself in 1915 for the printed article. The piece first ran in the San Francisco Chronicle as a long article. Praise from city and national men fills its opening pages in full.

Congressman Raker, author of the Raker bill, calls the piece clear and fine. Ex-mayor Phelan and board men of San Francisco add their thanks. Vilas lays out how the city would take water and power from the valley. That valley lies inside Yosemite National Park, the title page states. The fight over damming it was a live public question of the day. His case rests on study of the facts, the letters all agree.
68946-pausanias-description-of-greece-vo:
Pausanias's Description of Greece, volume one, is an English translation of a classic travel work. Arthur Shilleto made the translation, with notes and index. George Bell issued it in London in 1886. It belongs to Bohn's Classical Library. Pausanias lived in the age of the Antonines. He travelled all round Greece and wrote ten books. His tour describes what he saw and heard there.

The preface praises his record of Greek art. Every temple in his day was a museum of art, it says. Most of those works have since been swept away. His pages thus keep what no eye can see now. The work is also a mine of mythology. A quiet vein of humour runs through it. Later ages have used him as a guide to lost Greece. Volume one begins his tour of the cities.
69055-john-de-lancaster-a-novel-vol-i:
John de Lancaster is a novel in three volumes by Richard Cumberland, printed in London in 1809, and the hosted text is volume one. Cumberland says he raised no long lead in, since he had told of the book in his memoirs. He asks for a fair read.

The tale opens on March 1, 1751, at Kray Castle in North Wales. Robert De Lancaster, a man of great standing, feasts friends and neighbors for the day of their saint. The gentry eat well, and the poor are not left out. His son Philip has wed an heiress of the house of Morgan. A granddaughter, Cecilia, lost her mother young and bore long years with calm. Readers meet a Welsh family seat and the hero line at its root.
69337-music-as-a-human-need-a-plea-for-f:
Alma Webster Powell wrote Music as a Human Need, a plea for free national instruction in music, issued in New York in nineteen fourteen. The work was submitted for a doctor of philosophy degree in political science at Columbia University. Powell gave the work with gratitude to her husband, A Judson Powell. Two parts, appendices, and a bibliography fill the volume. Chapter one states the thesis.

Part one treats music and motion, group and individual reaction to music, and toneurology as a new branch of study. Part two treats music and national life in Italy, England, Germany, France, and the United States from eighteen hundred to nineteen thirteen. A preface notes a cold economic fact, that Chicago spent thirty million dollars in one year for instruments, sheet music, books, supplies, and lessons. Powell argues music is a need, not a luxury.
69657-itinerarium-curiosum-centuria-i:
William Stukeley, a doctor and fellow of learned societies, wrote an account of the antiquities and curiosities of nature and art seen in travels through Great Britain. A second edition of 1776 adds much material and copper plates. His preface says the work gives places and things from inspection. It is not compiled from other men's labors, or from travels in a study.

Stukeley calls it crude and hasty, like a traveler's notes. Many matters are hints for further scrutiny, he admits. He avoided prejudice and carried no author with him. His views on Roman stations differ from earlier writers because things appeared so to him. The prints serve as an index of inquiries for travelers.
71789-bones-and-i:
Bones and I, or The Skeleton at Home, by Whyte-Melville, is a book of musing talks with a skeleton. Ward, Lock printed it in London, with drawings by Forestier. The author had written Market Harborough and Katerfelto before this odd work.

A frontispiece shows the author contemplating his companion, the skeleton of the title. The chapters bear loose names: On Waste, Through the Mill, Gourds, and A Vampire. Gold for Silver, a day that is dead, and a four-leaved shamrock follow. The talk opens with a burst of questions fired at the skull. Why are the times out of joint, and is there any goal to it all, the narrator demands. He likens men to squirrels in a cage and pickpockets on a treadmill. A man who cut his throat from tiring of dressing and undressing gets a dark paragraph.
71905-the-discovery-and-decipherment-of-:
Arthur John Booth wrote The Discovery and Decipherment of the Trilingual Cuneiform Inscriptions, issued by Longmans, Green and Company in London, New York, and Bombay in nineteen oh two.
