Urban kept his predecessor's line toward the schismatics. Alexander Severus became emperor in 222, favouring religious eclecticism and protecting Christians. Lampridius stresses that Alexander made no trouble for Christians. Rome's church therefore enjoyed essential peace, though its legal status stayed unchanged. Claims that he converted many rest on Cecilia's Acts, and the silver-vessel tale is a later editor's invention. He probably died naturally, judging from the era's peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gennadius-:
Gennadius I, patriarch of Constantinople from 458 to 471, left scarcely any writings, yet his council's letter against simony survives. Facundus reports he wrote against Cyril of Alexandria about 431, more violently even than Ibas's letter, though Cyril's letter of 434 may show them friends by then. Succeeding Anatolius in 458, he received Leo's warning of 17 June 460 against Timothy Aelurus, Monophysite intruder at Alexandria. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows a patriarch known through others' letters.

Not later than 459 he gathered a council of eighty-one bishops, many from the East and Egypt, including men dispossessed by Aelurus. Its letter against simony, the buying of church office, is preserved in Mansi's collection. About the same time Daniel the Stylite mounted his column near the city, apparently without patriarchal leave. The entry sketches authority exercised through council and correspondence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-germanus-i:
Germanus I, patriarch of Constantinople from 715 to 730, lost his see for refusing an emperor's ban on images. Born at Constantinople late in Heraclius's reign to the noble Justinianus, he served at the cathedral, then became bishop of Cyzicus. At the synod of 712 he bowed with most Greek bishops to the emperor's new doctrine. True doctrine returned under Anastasius II. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 733 or 740.

As patriarch he defended the honour given to images in letters to Thomas of Claudiopolis and in debate with Constantine, whom he seemingly won over. Leo III pressed on, reading a volcanic eruption as judgment on idol worship and issuing his edict of 726. Germanus opposed him, won Gregory II's praise in 729, and in 730 refused to sign the imperial ban before a council. Forced to resign, he yielded to the pliant Anastasius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodosius-i:
Emperor Theodosius I, whom all call Great, ruled Rome's East with faith and iron will. Born in Spain about 346, he died at Milan on 17 January 395. He stamped out the last traces of pagan worship, ended Arian heresy in the empire, made peace with the Goths, and gave a famous show of penance for a crime. His father, General Comes Theodosius, and mother Thermantia were Catholics when Arianism stood at its height.

The son served well in the army, led Moesia as Dux, and beat the Sarmatians. His father's fall and death in 376 sent him home to Spain in disgrace. Gratian, after Valens died in 378, lifted him to fellow-emperor for the East on 19 January 379. Wed to Aelia Flacilla, father of Arcadius and Honorius, he ruled with law, faith, and a penitent heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valentinian-i:
Valentinian I, Flavius Valentinianus, ruled the West as emperor from 364 to 375. Born at Cibalis in Pannonia in 321 to humble parents, he entered the army young and became tribune of the scutarii about 360. He marched with Julian the Apostate to Antioch and was exiled to Gaul for refusing to honour idols. On Jovian's death he was proclaimed emperor on 26 February 364 and at once named his brother Valens ruler of the East.

He campaigned in Gaul against Alamanni and Burgundians, beating them at Châlons-sur-Marne, losing Mainz to them in 367, and overthrowing them at Solicinium at heavy cost. In 374 he made a treaty with their king Macrianus. The entry follows his reign, his religious tolerance, and his death at Bregetio near Pressburg on 17 November 375, during an audience with Quadi envoys.
cetywayo-and-his-white-neighbours-remark:
H. Rider Haggard first published his remarks on South Africa in 1882, three years after the Zulu war. He opens with speeches by Sir Garnet Wolseley and Lord Kimberley insisting Britain would never hand the Transvaal back. Against that fixed point he sets the history of Cetywayo, king of the Zulus, and the settlement imposed after his defeat.

Chaka, Dingaan, and Panda lead into Cetywayo's coronation, his army, and the war's causes. Haggard attacks Wolseley's settlement hard: carelessly chosen chiefs, fresh slaughter in Zululand, and a disappointed people. Natal colonists, Boer intentions, and the annexation of the Transvaal all come under review. The book argues policy from close knowledge of the ground.
chambers-s-elementary-science-readers-bo:
W. and R. Chambers built their Elementary Science Readers for the youngest schoolchildren, and Book I teaches by object lessons, each reading paired with a short lesson summary at the back. The cat comes first, in large simple words with accents marked: a child watches a cat wash, stretch, and slide out its claws from their sheaths.

Lessons move through the dog, buttercups and daisies, wheat, slate, and chalk, then on to the mouse, rabbit, ivy, bricks, and the donkey. Coffee, paper, the fly and wasp, the sunflower and rose all earn a page. Wood, coal, and fire end the course. Every common thing near a child's home becomes a first fact about the world.
collected-poems-1901-1918-in-two-volumes:
Collected Poems 1901–1918 in Two Volumes, Volume I, by Walter de la Mare, opens with the poems of The Listeners, 1914. A death-dream group leads, with Napoleon, England, and Truce among its titles. Characters from Shakespeare follow as short portraits: Falstaff, Macbeth, Iago, Ophelia, and Hamlet each get a poem.

Sonnets and Memories of Childhood fill the middle of the volume. The poems under the book's own title include Old Susan, Miss Loo, Arabia, The Dark Château, and The Listeners itself. A second gathering, Motley, 1918, closes the volume. Its titles turn stranger: The Little Salamander, The Sunken Garden, The Blind Boy, The Empty House, and The Revenant.
doe-osti-2574952-methodopt-a-shiny-based:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2024-00414, by Benjamin Luke and Stephanie Gamble in May 2025, introduces MethodOpt, a point-and-click tool for tuning lab instruments. Tools such as gas chromatograph mass spectrometers have many settings at once, and the best mix is found by trial. The usual one-setting-at-a-time approach is slow and misses how settings interact.

MethodOpt wraps a modern search method, one that tunes many settings toward several goals at once, in a Shiny web interface. Users lay out fractional factorial test plans, run variance analysis, and plot trade-offs without writing code. The approach saves substantial time and resources compared with older method development, the authors report. The tool was built under the laboratory's internal LDRD research program.
doe-osti-2584405-a-novel-sediment-passag:
Final technical report for award DE-EE0008947, from the University of Minnesota's St. Anthony Falls Laboratory under Jeffrey Marr, designs a passage for the river's own cargo: sediment. Dams trap sand that downstream reaches starve for, while reservoirs fill with the surplus. The project, February 2020 to September 2024, advanced a modular sediment bypass for new low-head hydropower, meant to keep sediment moving past the dam at something like its natural rate.

The team reviewed sand bed rivers and chose example sites, then iterated the module design across two budget periods with a go/no-go review between them. Readiness rose from TRL 2 to TRL 3 or 4. Partners included Barr Engineering, Utah State's Peter Wilcock, and Voigt Consultants. Design goals were threefold: stop reservoirs silting up, restore continuity of sediment transport, and prevent the scouring or buildup that unnatural sediment patterns cause downstream. The report archives how the design changed and why.
doe-osti-2587594-artificial-intelligence:
Dated August 10, 2025, this final scientific report closes Department of Energy award DE-EE0009212. The project applied artificial intelligence to transit agencies that run mixed fleets, with a focus on paratransit: the demand-response service that carries riders who book trips in advance or on the day. Scheduling those trips well is a hard problem that changes hour by hour.

The report tracks three phases. Algorithms cover an offline vehicle routing problem that knows some bookings ahead, a rolling horizon scheduler, and an online scheduling method for requests that arrive live. A simulation environment called Transit-Gym, extended as E-Transit Bench with electric grid simulation, let the team test ideas safely. Other threads improved rider occupancy estimation with neural networks and computer vision, built a paratransit web application, and engaged the community. Later chapters prepare a field test and review go/no-go milestones.
doe-osti-2588428-technologies-for-enhanc:
Matthew Searle, Owen Grabowski, and Douglas Straub of the National Energy Technology Laboratory wrote this technology review, DOE/NETL-2025/4938, dated July 9, 2025. Its subject is condensation inside supercritical carbon dioxide power cycles. How well the cooler condenses CO2 near its critical point strongly moves plant efficiency and the levelized cost of electricity, so better condenser surfaces pay off across the whole cycle.

The review surveys passive heat transfer enhancement: surfaces that boost condensation without moving parts. Established designs include helical micro-ribs inside tubes, documented in earlier literature. Newer options use additive manufacturing, such as conical pin arrays printed as part of the heat exchanger. Screening analysis and benchmark correlations compare the candidates, treating both stratified and annular two-phase flow regimes. The report closes with a recommended concept for enhanced condensation hardware in direct-fired sCO2 cycles.
doe-osti-2997304-exploring-transport-ena:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-12246, by Craig Hogle, Evan Johnson, Jonathan Sterk, Tharon Morrison, and Dan Stick, dated September 2025, works toward a scalable trapped-ion quantum computer. Ions held in traps serve as qubits, and light pulses steer them. The project combines two scaling ideas: shuttling ions between zones to run gates, and addressing them with light guides built into the chip.

Hardware chapters detail the pulse gear that times the shuttling. A simple pulser board fires trigger pulses to a digital-to-analog chassis when a move begins, without tracking the waveform details itself. Prior team results cited include high-fidelity ion operations with photonic modulators and multi-site optical addressing of trapped ions. The report assembles the control stack a larger ion machine will need.
doe-osti-2997654-simulations-of-radiatio:
University of Michigan final report on award DE-SC0023699, led by Carolyn Kuranz, covers simulation work from April 2023 to March 2025 on radiation flow in strongly coupled plasmas. In such plasmas the electric energy between ions beats their thermal energy, changing how radiation is absorbed and emitted. The physics runs from stellar interiors to shocks at the edges of forming galaxies.

The team built a ray-tracing program that follows radiation through a simulated neutron star capsule implosion, under conditions matched to Omega-60 laser experiments. The capsule was modeled in two dimensions as concentric rings of plastic, nickel, and helium, each with its own absorption and emission traits. Ray paths through the rings were derived on paper, then coded, and the rays were summed into the signal a distant detector would see. The short filing states the method and its target experiment.
doe-osti-2999078-isotopics-by-nuclides-t:
William Johnson of Sandia National Laboratories tests a gamma-spectrum analysis tool in report SAND2025-12717, printed September 2025. The tool, called Isotopics by Nuclides, sits inside InterSpec, a free program for reading radiation spectra. From a spectrum it estimates how much of each isotope a sample holds, the sort of answer inspectors need for uranium and plutonium checks.

Test cases used real measurements from an H3D M400 detector, a portable cadmium zinc telluride instrument. Uranium and plutonium runs were checked first, then a mixed sample of highly enriched and low enriched uranium. A harder case was simulated: a solid sphere of 90 percent enriched uranium wrapped in depleted uranium, generated with the GADRAS code. One tuned setting, shipped as a preset, handled each family of spectra. The report records where the tool reads enrichment well and where shielding or mixing strains it.
doe-osti-3000610-implementation-of-a-tur:
Chris Chartrand of Sandia National Laboratories reports a laboratory-directed project in SAND2025-13481R, printed September 2025, that puts wind farms inside a global climate model. Wind farms have spread widely, yet their full effect on Earth systems is poorly known. Each turbine steals momentum from the wind and stirs turbulence behind it, and thousands together might nudge rain, soil moisture or even the jet stream.

The project implemented a turbine farm model in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, the big coupled simulator that joins atmosphere, ocean and land chemistry. The new module extracts momentum from the modelled airflow wherever farms stand. With it, scientists can run decades-long simulations and watch precipitation, extreme weather, soil moisture and jet stream position respond. The tool is meant to inform where farms get built, weighing clean energy gains against real effects on the natural systems around them.
doe-osti-3006948-integrating-cyber-infor:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/CON-25-88262, by Benjamin Lampe and Russell Gold and dated September 30, 2025, explains how cyber-informed engineering fits into process automation. The approach starts from the physical harm an attack could cause, then designs the control system so that harm cannot happen. Programmable logic controllers, the small computers that run plant equipment, get close attention throughout.

Working through the CIE principles one by one, the authors show how engineers can add system-wide protections. They question digital features the plant does not need and keep manual or physical fallbacks in place. The method is also tied to federal risk rules that plants must meet to win an authorization to operate. Plant engineers get a practical route to safer automated systems.
doe-osti-3011876-a-comprehensive-study-o:
Inverter based units change how protection relays behave. Jing Wang and Andy Hoke of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, with University of Idaho coauthors, tested generic inverter models and control choices against relay elements used on transmission systems. Both grid following and grid forming style controls enter the analysis. Relay elements are the parts of a protection relay that sense faults and trip breakers.

Time domain elements get a close look. The incremental quantity distance element TD21 needs its operating signal to exceed the restraining signal, of opposite sign. The directional element TD32 guards permissive overreaching transfer trip schemes. The November 2025 report works element by element through the consequences.
doe-osti-3013245-guidance-for-grid-resil:
NREL authors Reiko Matsuda-Dunn, Jordan Burns, Abodh Poudyal, and five colleagues wrote this November 2025 guidance on grid resilience decisions for rural Minnesota. Rural electric cooperatives run long distribution lines through storm country with small staffs and tight budgets. The report identifies which weather hazards hit Minnesota distribution systems hardest and how utilities currently choose resilience investments.

Outage and grid data came from seven participating electric cooperatives. The analysis links wind-related outages to line and pole attributes and reviews the metrics utilities use, or lack, in planning. A long section catalogs which customers depend most on power, from people on medical devices to shelters and public safety sites. The guidance aims to help small utilities defend resilience spending with evidence.
doe-osti-3013781-num-dat-file-format-spe:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-20193, by John Lang Jr., William Anderson, Frank Cherne, Rachel Huber, and Michael Hargather, issued January 12, 2026, specifies the NUM-DAT file format used to archive data from the M-9 gun experiments. M-9 is Los Alamos's Shock and Detonation Physics group, which fires gas guns to study how materials behave under extreme pressure. Consistent archiving keeps decades of shot data readable.

The specification defines the structure of the group's .num and .dat files so any analyst can parse them the same way. A comparison table places the format beside alternatives the group encounters: Nevada Test Site .dig files, comma-separated text, Tektronix oscilloscope waveforms, and MATLAB files. Worked example data and a MATLAB reader in the appendix let new staff validate their own tools.
doe-osti-3015015-toward-automated-plasma: Automated calibration of a plasma focused ion beam instrument is the subject of a July 24, 2025 SULI poster by Emerson Liu with Hoffmann, Gannon, and Spurgeon. Computer vision scores spot burns cut into silicon, giving figures of merit for astigmatism, quad, and focus. A UNet++ model segments the burns from microscope images, reaching a stig score of 0.9128 on the example shown. As a single-page poster, it gives the approach and early results rather than a full study; future work adds focus and quad scores and more training data.
doe-osti-3015064-the-manufacture-of-adva:
NLR/TP-6A50-96472, dated January 2026, is the MAKE IT Prize final technical report. Holly and Sweet wrote it. Domestic energy manufacturing is its subject. The prize paid teams to plan and ready factories for key energy systems inside the United States.

Two tracks ran in parallel. Facilities Track winners first produced a sound plan for a plant. They then proved themselves shovel-ready. Site control, permits, financing, and community backing were all in hand. The Strategies Track rewarded new manufacturing joint ventures across regions. Winners ranged from Beatrice, Nebraska to Pittsfield, Massachusetts and Riverside, California. Support came through Power Connectors in the American-Made network. They ran peer exchanges, matchmaking webinars, and expert sessions free to competitors.
doe-osti-3015716-assembly-and-repair-of-:
Louisiana State University's final technical report for award DE-SC0020119 covers a project led by David J Vinyard from September 2019 to August 2024. The subject is Photosystem II, the protein complex that uses sunlight to split water in plants and related organisms. The team studied how this complex is built, and how damaged copies get taken apart and repaired.

Work ran along three lines: protein contacts that help assembly, the chemistry that builds the manganese-calcium oxygen-evolving complex, and the steps that mark worn centers for breakdown. Methods included electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, protein chemistry, genetics, mass spectrometry, and computer modeling. Results show that proton release limits early assembly steps, while chloride and calcium ions help manganese oxidation. The findings matter for anyone designing artificial photosynthesis systems.
doe-osti-3017119-transitions-dynamics-an:
Thomas F Rosenbaum of the California Institute of Technology wrote this revised final report for award DE-SC0014866. The project studied transitions, dynamics, and driven states in quantum magnets. Its test system was a physical version of the transverse-field Ising model, a standard model of magnetism where a sideways magnetic field acts as a quantum tuning knob.

The team probed collective electronuclear modes at a quantum phase transition in pure and disordered ferromagnets. They traced behavior from single spin flips to whole domain tunneling in a ferromagnet driven around its hysteresis loop. Quantum and classical annealing runs were compared through their fluctuation spectra. Tools included ac and dc magnetometry, Barkhausen noise measurement, and microwave studies. The work speaks to basic questions about stability, coherence, and control in quantum materials, with an eye on future quantum devices.
doe-osti-3019572-m3as-25in1002073-analys:
Timothy Le Phero, Bibo Zhong, Michael D McMurtrey, and five colleagues at Idaho National Laboratory analyzed irradiated strain gauges in INL/RPT-25-89342, December 2025. The gauges were printed, not machined: silver nanoparticle ink on aluminum substrates, insulated with polyimide tape 25 micrometers thick. Printing promises conformal sensors for reactor internals. The question is whether they survive the environment they would measure. Irradiation testing ran at Ohio State's research reactor. Fixtures carried thermocouples to log temperature through the exposure.

The report's job is the data: what the gauges read under irradiation, and how far those readings can be trusted. Fabrication details, from ink choice to encapsulation, are documented so the results can be reproduced. Printed sensors that drift under neutron flux are curiosities; printed sensors with characterized drift are instruments. This analysis moves the gauges from the first class toward the second. Milestone M3AS-25IN1002073 is the deliverable the report closes.
doe-osti-3022719-equipment-assessment-gu:
INL guide INL/RPT-26-89297, from the Center for Securing Digital Energy Technology, gives power grid asset owners a step-by-step method. It covers inspecting and hardening the operational technology devices their systems depend on. Field devices and embedded systems are frequent cyber targets. Many owners have no structured way to check what is actually inside the boxes on their poles and in their substations.

The procedure walks through asset identification and verification, physical security and tamper inspection, firmware integrity checks, configuration baseline audits, port and communication security, and user account and access control. Practical requirements follow the standards. One example is monitoring vendor remote access sessions and alerting on new logins, as CIP-005-6 requires. Another is funneling vendor connections through jump hosts in a demilitarized zone rather than granting broad network reach.
doe-osti-3023092-digital-assurance-for-g:
Idaho National Laboratory brief INL/RPT-26-90975, issued January 2026, is the second Digital Assurance Brief from the lab's Center for Securing Digital Energy Technology. Megan Jordan Culler, Remy Vanece Stolworthy, Alex Tylecote, and co-authors take up a fast-growing strain on the power grid: very large new electric loads asking to connect. Keeping the grid reliable now depends on digital systems behaving as promised.

The brief draws lessons from the rollout of inverter-based resources, whose modeling troubles carry clear parallels for large loads. A dynamics working group view is quoted: interconnecting load owners should supply composite or user-defined models of their sites, alongside standard models still in development. Accurate models, the authors argue, remain an unsolved need for grid-impacting equipment.
doe-osti-3025714-international-collabora:
Jens Birkholzer, LianGe Zheng, and Boris Faybishenko of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report a year of international collaboration on geologic disposal of spent fuel and high-level waste, LBNL-2001723, dated December 5, 2025. Countries building deep repositories share experiments in underground labs such as Grimsel in Switzerland, since no nation wants to learn every lesson alone. This FY25 progress report is peer reviewed.

Bentonite buffer tests, run under the HotBENT program, get detailed modeling attention. Sweden's SKB built thermal models in Comsol starting in 2023, then coupled thermal, hydrologic, and mechanical behavior in 2024, and Clay Technology added two-dimensional models. The coupled models matched the first laboratory experiment decently, but gaps between model and data remain for the second. Berkeley's own FY25 modeling of that case is set out in a companion section.
doe-osti-3168349-midwest-zevi-2030-charg:
Cummins, Purdue University, and the two national laboratories behind this April 2026 roadmap plan truck charging along the I-80 corridor under award DE-EE0010648. The Midwest ZEVI project covers Indiana, Illinois, and Ohio, plus the wider Indiana highway network. Medium- and heavy-duty zero-emission trucks promise lower running costs and less fossil fuel use, but fleets will not buy them without public chargers sized for big rigs on long routes.

Two lab tools drive the study. POLARIS, an Argonne agent-based traffic simulator, traces freight trips and energy use across the network. EVI-Pro HD, from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, then sites and sizes the chargers those trips need. Fleet surveys and stakeholder sessions feed the runs, and financial chapters test utilization paths and operating cost guesses.
doe-osti-3362961-soft-x-ray-vuv-diagnost: Kevin Tritz of Johns Hopkins University files this short final report under grant DE-SC0021207, covering September 2020 to August 2025, on X-ray diagnostics for the NSTX-U tokamak at Princeton. Machine upgrade delays, COVID disruption, and staff losses shrank the scope to refurbishing the soft X-ray and vacuum ultraviolet instruments. Both poloidal arrays got new diode sensors and fresh beryllium filters, and the multi-energy system was rebuilt, bench tested, and mounted. The ultraviolet spectrometer was validated at Johns Hopkins and handed to the Princeton crew for later installation.
doe-osti-3365082-signal-to-background-es:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-24030, by René Reifarth, Aaron Couture, Ingrid Knapová, Andrew L. Cooper, and Shea M. Mosby, estimates signal and background for a planned neutron capture experiment at LANSCE. The setup inverts the usual geometry: a beam of krypton-78 ions, accelerated to about 60 keV, passes through a neutron target, and some ions capture a neutron to become krypton-79. Rates of this reaction feed models of how heavy elements form in stars.

Simulations compare two moderator designs, plain carbon and a beryllium-carbon mix, that slow neutrons around the ion pipe. After 0.1 milliseconds only thermal neutrons remain in the pipe, and none are left after 10 milliseconds. Expected signal and background counts under stated beam assumptions decide whether the proof-of-principle run can see the reaction above noise.
doe-osti-3366926-mechanical-characteriza:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2019852, by Connor Clary of UC Davis and dated June 2026, investigates a small flexure with outsized influence on fusion targets. In the National Ignition Facility's target assembly, sixteen silicon pads bond to an aluminum can through a fixture whose compliant flexure sets bond force. Bondline thickness must hold within plus or minus 4 micrometers, so flexure stiffness must be predictable.

A run of low bond strength assemblies triggered the study. Flexures built to one specification measured at varying stiffness, and the values did not always follow the presumed beam mechanics model. The report rebuilds the geometry mathematically, including rounded end transitions, to compute force more accurately, and checks whether earlier stiffness measurements were trustworthy. Two questions organize it: does the fixture work as intended, and were the measurements right?
doe-osti-3374533-acceleration-of-thermoc:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-25-87425, dated August 2025, speeds up chemistry solves inside two lab simulation codes. The authors are Parikshit Bajpai, Chaitanya Vivek Bhave, and Daniel Schwen. Their codes, MOOSE and Pronghorn, model reactors such as molten salt designs. At each step the codes ask Thermochimica to find the chemical balance of hot fuel and coolant. Those calls are slow, and they run millions of times.

The team attacked the cost three ways. They added multi-threading support for the chemistry solver. They cached values so repeat states skip fresh solves. They also filled gaps by interpolation, weighing nearby states or using point weights inside a simplex. A molten salt fast reactor off-gassing case shows the speed gains. The work sits in the NEAMS advanced modeling program.
doe-osti-3375375-lawrence-livermore-nati:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's Innovation and Partnerships Office issued its fiscal 2024 technology transfer report as LLNL-TR-2007984. Melissa Lewelling, the office's communications manager, is the named contact. The report is a glossy yearbook of how lab science reaches the market. It counts licenses, deals, and awards for fiscal 2024. New staff profiles and program updates fill the front half.

Success stories fill the back half. BridgeBio Oncology works on cancer drugs built on lab science. A-Alpha Bio uses a lab tie-up to map protein interplay. EVOQ Therapeutics applies lab nanolipoprotein tech to autoimmune care. A space story covers GEOStare SV2, a joint build with Terran Orbital. A fusion hub story pairs the lab with Longview. An awards section honors in-house teams, among them the EXUDE Elite optics group and the UMap and UnifyFS software teams.
doe-osti-3376453-final-report-accelerati:
A final report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0023892 closes a University of Arizona project led by Tim Eifler on neural network shortcuts for cosmology. Surveys such as DES, DESI, and the coming LSST produce data vectors whose theory matches take heavy computing. The team trained networks to stand in for the slow codes. One suite grew out of the CosmoLike frame and covers paired probes: galaxy lensing, clustering, baryon acoustic wiggles, cluster counts, and microwave background maps.

A second suite speeds the UniverseMachine galaxy model. A 2025 paper by Bowden and Behroozi came from that strand. Their network reads a galaxy and its setting, then calls whether it is a central or a satellite. It also flags past fly-bys and current infall. A third suite emulates the covariance matrices that weight every fit. Graduate student Joe Adamo published on that piece.
doe-osti-3377372-comments-on-the-paper-e:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229894-2026-TECH, by A. Poblaguev and dated June 2026, takes issue with a paper on beam-induced depolarization in the Electron-Ion Collider's hydrogen jet target. The jet target is the yardstick for proton beam polarimetry at the collider. If the beam scrambles the target's atoms, the yardstick bends. The paper claims a way to remove that effect. Poblaguev argues steps do not hold.

Three faults lead the critique. First, the claim of transitions within 2.38 megahertz of a harmonic clashes with the superposition principle. Each part of the drive field acts on its own; off-resonant parts cannot force resonant jumps. Second, the Rabi frequency used is a scaled measure, not a dynamic frequency. Third, the harmonic cutoff of 55.8 has no power to predict. The photon rate curves serve for checks between setups, the note grants. It marks this as Part I of the comments.
doe-osti-3377444-machine-learning-guided:
An internship report from Idaho National Laboratory, by Christie Djidjev of the University of Texas at Austin and dated September 23, 2025, tackles conflict in open radio access networks. In O-RAN, control apps called xApps each tune network settings in near real time. Apps from mixed vendors act without sight of each other. Their clashes can wreck call quality. Djidjev's task: learn which settings drive which key performance indicators.

The method turns data into yes-no form. Decision trees binarize each parameter and indicator. Then a Boolean matrix holds the links from settings to outcomes. Solving Boolean matrix equations over sliding time windows recovers that matrix as the network shifts. When the fit sours, the matrix updates. A mobile handover case tests the scheme. It recovers the links with good accuracy. Rules stay readable for engineers, unlike black-box models. The aim is conflict warning for operators.
doe-osti-3377905-e2c-cohort-on-major-ene:
Bandana Kar presents the E2C Cohort on Major Energy Disruptions in the Southeast in slides dated May 21, 2026, from the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The workshop weighs trade-offs and feasibility of energy investment for community resilience. Participants learn to compare two costs. One is the cost of preventing outage damage. The other is the cost of responding to a disaster after it lands.

Resilience is defined as a system's ability to anticipate, prepare for, and adapt to changing conditions. It must then withstand, respond to, and recover rapidly from disruptions. A cost table grades the options. Distribution automation upgrades support distributed resources and microgrids but need ongoing operations spending. Microgrids carry moderate capital cost and complex ownership and tariff questions. Diesel and gas generators deploy fast but depend on fuel supply. Battery backup is limited in duration.
doe-osti-3382181-comments-on-the-paper-e:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229973-2026-TECH, by A. Poblaguev and dated June 2026, is Part II of a comment on a published paper. The paper concerns the hydrogen jet target at the Electron-Ion Collider. It proposed eliminating beam-induced depolarizing effects in the target, which serves high-precision proton beam polarimetry. Comments of this kind test a result's arithmetic in public.

The note works through the target's storage cell and feeding tube geometry. It compares measured beam profile widths in the two directions, about 6.38 and 6.84 millimeters, which agree within errors and give a common width near 6.73 millimeters. From that width it estimates the fraction of beam intensity reaching the compression tube. Atoms move at a speed set by a temperature of 65 kelvin. Molecules scattered and recombined on chamber walls sit at 290 kelvin. The note also checks a coefficient of 0.67 against the cited reference.
doe-osti-3383512-los-alamos-national-lab:
Jillian Grubenhoff's co-op work experience report, Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-26363 issued July 23, 2026, accounts for her summer 2026 research and development internship at the laboratory. The report was written for course ENGR 3190 at Texas State University's Ingram School of Engineering. It was presented to Dr. Michelle Londa. Austin Sutton, the laboratory engineer who supervised the placement, approved it.

The abstract frames the report as a record of duties, outcomes, and project details from the internship. It also carries an important limit. Specific project information is designated Controlled Unclassified Information under export control rules. That covers numerical results, experiment configurations, and photographs. Only content reviewed and cleared for open release appears in the document. The public version therefore describes the experience at the level the laboratory cleared, and no deeper.
doe-osti-3398818-full-waveform-inversion:
Arthur Rodgers of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's Geophysical Monitoring Program reports a new three-dimensional model of the lithosphere under northwest China and its neighbors in LLNL-TR-2022202, dated July 24, 2026. The method is full waveform inversion tomography. It fits whole seismic waveforms rather than just arrival times. The data are open broadband records.

The work starts from a simple isotropic model that honors crustal thickness and long-wavelength topography. From there, the inversion infers radially anisotropic wavespeed structure across northwest China, western Mongolia, and eastern Kazakhstan. The resulting model images strong sideways changes that match known tectonic provinces. It fits observed waveforms far better than other models do. Better earth models of this kind sharpen the monitoring of distant seismic events. That monitoring is the program's reason for building them.
doe-osti-3403168-high-temperature-sic-cl:
In August 2026, Oak Ridge National Laboratory released report ORNL/SPR-2026/4722, which sets out an irradiation test for silicon carbide end plugs used on fuel cladding. Daniel Hott, Nicholas Russell, Dillon Cranford, Takaaki Koyanagi, and Christian M. Petrie wrote the design study. The test will run in the High Flux Isotope Reactor, called HFIR.

Plugs will face a fast neutron flux at about 300 degrees Celsius, near light-water reactor heat levels. The goal is to check whether the plugs stay sealed and strong after irradiation. Thermal studies tune holder size and fill gas, using 90 percent helium in one case, to hold the right sample heat.
doe-osti-3412016-evaluating-micromobilit:
Slide deck by Sailesh Acharya and Bingrong Sun of the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated August 2026, grades how easy small vehicles and bikes are to use in Greeley, Colorado. The study uses traffic stress levels and a score called MEP, for mobility energy productivity.

One case upgrades 11th Avenue and tracks the change across the city. Citywide MEP improved by 36 percent in that scenario. Gains spread across town, shaped by streets and land use. Planners can see which street fixes open the most trips to people who do not drive.
far-off-or-asia-and-australia-described-:
Mortimer's Far Off describes Asia and Australia for young Christian readers. Favell Lee Mortimer also wrote The Peep of Day, the title page notes. This New York issue is dated 1852. Anecdotes and illustrations carry the geography throughout.

The frontispiece shows an English lady teaching on Mount Sion. She leads Jewish and Muslim girls beyond Jerusalem's gates to learn of the Saviour. Little Esther, a Jewess of eight, sings of Christ as our Redeemer. The scene states the book's missionary frame at once. Description of lands and peoples follows in that spirit. Customs, scenes, and stories aim to interest children in distant places. Mortimer writes the world as a field for Christian teaching.
female-scripture-biography-volume-i:
Cox sets out to honor the women of the Bible in Female Scripture Biography, Volume I. Francis Augustus Cox wrote the book, and the Boston edition here is dated 1831. It pairs lives of women from scripture with an essay on what Christianity has done for women. His preface argues that books of devotion can hardly be too many, since taste varies so much.

Each life takes a woman of the Old or New Testament and draws out her story and its lessons. The sampled pages turn to Israel in the time of the judges. Cox quotes the book of Nehemiah on a people who would not hear. Then he takes up Jabin, king of Canaan, raised up in his telling to trouble a land whose faith had faded. Verse, tale, and moral run side by side through the volume.
for-the-faith-a-story-of-the-young-pione:
Everett-Green tells of the young Oxford scholars who first spread Reformation teaching in England. Her notes name John Clarke and Henry Sumner, who died from harsh imprisonment, unreconciled to the church they had offended. Clarke, she judges, would have gone to the stake had death not taken him first.

The undergraduate Dalaber wavers between two leaders. Garret blazes with fire and fine resolutions about martyrdom, yet his nerve fails before peril. Clarke stands quiet and immovable, conscience clear, ready to be found at his post. Evelyn Everett-Green shapes their circle, the Christian Brothers, through flight, prison, and the fire at Carfax.
frank-reynolds-r-i:
Johnson presents the black-and-white art of Frank Reynolds, with forty-six examples in brush, pen, and pencil. The volume belongs to a series meant to rescue press illustration from its ephemeral life. Reynolds drew for the illustrated papers that most readers threw away.

His gift, the essay argues, is a saving grace of humour and a quizzical interest in fellow men. Belgravia's foibles and Bethnal Green's broader humours please him equally. In the Dinners with Shakespeare cartoons he touched off the mannerisms of the dinner-table. A. E. Johnson suggests future historians of the age will mine such drawings for the look of society.
freytag-pictures-of-german-life-xviiixix:
Modern Germany takes shape in the first volume of Freytag's Pictures of German Life for the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, in English. Frederick the Great, the Napoleonic wars, and the rise of the middle class mark the road. Freytag traces change in homes and workshops as much as in ideas and battles.

Enlightenment talk in coffee houses gives way to factories, railways, and new professions. He watches manners, dress, and family life shift as the old estates loosen their grip. Lively and opinionated, the history argues that Germany became modern from the household outward. The novelist's eye for character keeps abstractions grounded in people. Readers finish with a felt sense of two centuries of daily transformation.
freytag-pictures-of-german-life-xvxvii-c:
German daily life from the 1400s through the 1600s fills the first volume of Gustav Freytag's Pictures of German Life, presented here in English. The Reformation, the peasants' wars, and the Thirty Years' War pass across these pages. Freytag tells the great events through homes, workshops, and market squares rather than battlefields alone.

Costume, craft, food, and faith receive the novelist's eye for telling detail. Ordinary people carry three crowded centuries in this telling. The volume made cultural history popular in Germany, a genre Freytag practically founded there. Rich in fact and warm in sympathy, it brings its centuries vividly to life. Historians still respect the research under the readable surface.
george-washington-volume-i:
Henry Cabot Lodge wrote this life of Washington for the American Statesmen series, first published in 1889. Volume I carries Washington from his Virginia youth through the French and Indian War and into the Revolution. Lodge, a historian who later sat in the Senate, had the Stuart portrait of Washington set as the frontispiece.

The volume dwells on the making of the man: the surveyor, the planter, the young officer who learned hard lessons on the frontier. War chapters follow him to Boston, New York, and the long fight for independence. Lodge writes in a formal, admiring style, with an eye on Washington's growth in judgment. Readers get the first half of a stately two-volume life, ending as peace comes in view.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DomesticIntelli: nsia-DomesticIntelligenceKing Domestic Intelligence King: the made public government document on domestic intelligence and King, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-InvestigationKi:
An FBI investigative report from the Memphis office, dated June 10, 1968, covers the hunt for Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s killer. Its span runs from April 4, the day King was shot in Memphis, to June 10. Two months of a national manhunt are gathered into one office's account.

Memphis was the office of origin because the crime happened on its ground. Reports like this one collected interviews, leads, and arrests into the case's spine. By June 10 the search had reached its end in an arrest abroad, and the report closes that first phase of the case.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_korea-nu:
Under President George H.W. Bush, the United States tried an opening diplomatic strategy toward North Korea. Robert A. Wampler edited this briefing book, number 610, published in November 2017. Declassified documents show Defense Secretary Dick Cheney warning allies about moving too fast toward force.

Cheney told partners that military force could jeopardize the initial diplomatic approach to Pyongyang. At the same time Washington had to keep Seoul aligned on political, diplomatic, and security interests. That balancing act, pressure beside engagement, defined Korea policy for decades. The early 1990s version is preserved here in the participants' own paper.
grace-harlowe-s-junior-year-at-high-scho:
Jessie Graham Flower's third High School Girls book, copyrighted in 1911, carries Grace Harlowe into her junior year. The frontispiece shows Grace snatching off a white mask. Early chapters bring a new arrival, confidences, and an autumn walking expedition. Then Grace makes a discovery, and the Phi Sigma Tau sorority takes the stage. Eleanor, a girl with a claim of artistic temperament, throws down the gauntlet.

A rescue party, a sacred duty performed by Julia, and schoolgirl plots fill the year. Flower's sorority is a test of loyalty: fast friends must stand by each other against snobbery and spite. Grace leads by kindness and nerve, as her readers expected. The book is a period piece of American school life, when secret societies in high schools were a live question and a rich source of story.
helbeck-of-bannisdale-volume-i:
Mrs Humphry Ward wrote this novel of faith and doubt in two volumes. Volume I brings Laura Fountain to a bleak northern valley. There she meets Mr Helbeck, a strict Catholic landowner. His cold, set faith clashes with her free and lively spirit at once.

The first three books build the clash in slow, close scenes. Village children, priests, and kin watch the pair draw near and pull apart. Ward asks what a person owes to belief, and what belief can cost. This volume sets up the bond and the strain that the second volume must resolve.
illustrated-catalogue-of-the-collections:
James Stevenson compiled this illustrated catalogue of goods obtained from the Indians of New Mexico in 1880. It appeared in the Bureau of Ethnology report printed in Washington in 1883. Towns covered include Cuyamunque, Nambe, Pojuaque, Santa Clara, and Tesuque. Santo Domingo and a turquoise mine also appear.

Entries sort finds by stone, clay, bone, and plant matter. Black polished ware and white ware with colored designs get close note. Each item has a number and a short note on form and wear. The list preserves what was gathered, town by town, in that year.
iranian-influence-on-moslem-literature-p:
Konstantin Inostrantzev wrote Iranian Influence on Moslem Literature, Part I, rendered from the Russian by G. K. Nariman in 1918. Chapters treat Arabic writers as sources for Sasanian culture. Parsi clergy preserving tradition come next. Ethical books of the Arabs are traced to Iranian origin alone.

Arab translators from Pahlavi and the Pahlavi books they studied fill the middle. Appendices add the trial of Afshin and the letter of Tansar. A merchant with a house full of aloe wood serves a parable on the next world. The book maps Persia's gift to Arabic letters.
joy-a-play-on-the-letter-i:
Joy is a three-act play by John Galsworthy, subtitled A Play on the Letter I. Its people gather at Colonel Hope's house near the Thames, above Oxford. The colonel and his wife, their old governess Miss Beech, and their daughter Letty head the cast. Letty's husband Ernest, their niece Mrs. Gwyn, and her daughter Joy complete the family.

The whole action passes on one midsummer day, on a lawn under a huge old beech tree. A swing, a low wall, and roses set the scene. Guests include Dick Merton and the Honorable Maurice Lever. The title points at Joy herself and at the letter I: selfishness at play among pleasant people. Galsworthy treats his country-house company with a light, comic hand.
leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-i:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Leila tells of the siege of Granada. Book One opens in the summer of 1491. Ferdinand and Isabel's armies have surrounded the city.

Moonlight falls on the Spanish camp and the Sierra Nevada. The first chapter pairs an enchanter with a warrior. A king in his palace and young lovers follow. Leila, a Jewish maiden, stands at the story's heart. Her father and her faith pull her toward danger. Lytton builds historical romance from Spain's last Moorish war. Almamen the enchanter gives the tale a magical thread. Granada's palace scenes mix splendor with quiet dread.
letters-from-high-latitudes-being-some-a:
Lord Dufferin wrote Letters from High Latitudes about a northern voyage in 1856. His yacht was the Foam. The first letter is dated from Glasgow on Monday, June 2, 1856.

The start went badly, he admits at once. A telegram told him the Foam had put into Holyhead. His master of the yacht had fallen suddenly ill. The season was short, so delay threatened the whole expedition. Dufferin's lively letters carry readers toward Iceland and beyond. Iceland, Jan Mayen, and Spitzbergen lay on his route north. A young lord's yacht voyage became a Victorian favorite.
letters-of-horace-walpole-volume-i:
Volume One of Horace Walpole's letters covers the years 1736 to 1764. T. Fisher Unwin published it in London, with Putnam's in New York. The first letter, to Montagu in May 1736, treats a royal marriage.

Early letters share Eton memories and a wish to travel. Paris theatres, French manners, and gambling amuse the young Walpole. His letters sparkle with gossip, jokes, and sharp character sketches. Walpole became the great letter writer of his age. This volume shows that gift forming, letter by letter. Later letters in this volume reach the 1760s. Strawberry Hill, his playful Gothic house, begins to rise in them.
maximilian-in-mexico-a-woman-s-reminisce:
Sara Yorke Stevenson wrote Maximilian in Mexico from her own memories. Her tale covers the French move into Mexico from 1862 to 1867. The Century Company held the rights from 1897 to 1899.

She first told the tale in five pieces in Century Magazine in 1897. The book honors Matias Romero, Mexico's minister to Washington. Part one treats the Triple Alliance of 1861 and 1862. Later parts treat Puebla, the French in the capital, and the empire of Maximilian. She wrote as one of the last folk left from that drama. Her nearness to events gives the book its chief value.
memoirs-of-margaret-fuller-ossoli-volume:
Volume one of the Memoirs of Margaret Fuller Ossoli came out in Boston. Phillips, Sampson and Company printed it, with rights entered in 1851. R. F. Fuller entered those rights in Massachusetts that year.

Lines from Ben Jonson head the book, on a learned and manly soul. Lines from Leonardo da Vinci stand beside them in Italian. The title names her Ossoli, the name she bore at her death. Friends built these memoirs from her papers after that loss, in two volumes. A full contents list for the first volume follows those lines. Her youth and growth fill the early parts of the memoir.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner opens his folklore set along the Hudson and its hills. Rip Van Winkle stands first in this first volume's list. Catskill gnomes, a witch, and the Devil's Dance-Chamber follow. The Galloping Hessian and the Storm Ship sail close behind.

Dutch settlers left rich tales along this river valley. Skinner adds Indian lore and tales of the Revolution. Anthony's Nose and Dunderberg give the hills their own ghosts. A baker's dozen and a culprit fay lighten the dread. The volume proves America's own backyard held old, weird tales to match any in Europe.
nasa-tm-19660012905-factors-affecting-fa:
David White and a colleague at Ames, in the exobiology division, studied how yeast preparations build fatty acids without whole cells. The yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the common baking and brewing yeast. Cell-free preparations let scientists watch the chemistry step by step. Earlier work in the same laboratory had shown that fatty acid synthesis in yeast is strongly influenced by certain factors, the authors note.

Naming those factors helps explain how living cells make fats. Fats store energy and build cell walls in every organism. A space agency studied such basic life chemistry as part of its biology program. White's work supported the broader study of life that also drove the search beyond Earth.
nasa-tm-19660013867-machining-and-grindi:
C T Olofson, F W Boulger, and J A Gurkis compiled this study of cutting titanium, dated August 4, 1965. It was prepared under the Redstone Scientific Information Center. The sponsor was the Army Missile Command at Marshall. Titanium is strong and light, but it is famously hard to machine well. Cutting, grinding, and other metal removal work on titanium and its alloys are all covered.

Titanium grabs tools, heats quickly, and can spoil a part late in making. Shops needed shared, tested guidance rather than local habit. A compiled study gathers what many shops had learned the hard way. Missile and aircraft builders of the era depended on titanium parts, so machining knowledge had direct weight in cost and quality.
nasa-tm-19660030683-a-high-strength-nick:
William J. Waters and John C. Freche, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, report a new metal in this paper. The metal is a nickel-base alloy built for hot turbine parts. It keeps high strength while resisting oxidation, the crusting attack of hot air, at temperatures up to 2200 degrees Fahrenheit.

The authors prepared the paper for a gas turbine conference in Houston in March 1967. In it, they present the alloy as an answer to a hard trade-off. Turbine parts want strength at extreme heat, but many strong alloys corrode fast there. An alloy that holds both strength and oxidation resistance could serve longer in hot engine sections.
nasa-tm-19670007216-an-experiment-to-det:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center issued this report in December 1966. It describes an experiment built to catch living microorganisms high in the atmosphere, where almost no sampling had been done. A cosmic dust collector was modified for the job and flown on the Aerobee sounding rocket flight NASA 4.150, on September 28, 1965.

After recovery, samples were checked two ways: by classical growth methods and by the firefly luciferase test for adenosine triphosphate. That molecule is found in living cells. Neither method gave statistically significant evidence that microorganisms were present. The report also documents sterility checks on the collector, sampling film, and handling procedures, along with flight conditions and sample volume. Future flights, it says, will need larger samples and better assay sensitivity.
nasa-tm-19670014635-on-the-ion-compositi:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center issued this paper in December 1966 on the topside ionosphere, the upper region of Earth's ionized atmosphere. Up there, electrons, ions, and neutral gases are not in thermal balance, and oxygen ions far outnumber hydrogen ions. The paper asks how those ions are distributed with height, and how hot the plasma runs.

A computer program solves the particle continuity equations for hydrogen and oxygen ions together with the energy equation. Included processes range from photoionization and charge exchange to diffusion along magnetic field lines and heat loss from ions to neutrals. Boundary values came from Explorer XXII measurements. The results map the transition region where oxygen ions give way to hydrogen ions. That level sits near eight hundred kilometers over the equator at midday and sinks at night.
nasa-tm-19670029798-x-ray-optics-part-i:
J. Mangus, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in September 1967. It is Part I of a series reporting Goddard's research on glancing incidence optical components. X-rays reflect only at shallow glancing angles, so X-ray telescopes use nested curved mirrors rather than ordinary lenses. The work came from Goddard's Optics Branch.

This report concentrates on the theory and design of a two-element glancing incidence telescope. Mangus analyzes Goddard's X-ray telescope experiment built for the Apollo Telescope Mount, a design pairing a concave parabola with a concave hyperbola. His tool is a modified ray tracing program. Image quality improves significantly, he shows, when the detector matches the optimum focal surface. Blocking rays that flare the image also helps, and trimming the second mirror to about half length halves its weight. That saves material cost and fabrication time.
nasa-tm-19680026278-the-influence-of-var:
J. R. Herman and S. Chandra of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this theoretical study, dated July 1966, on how varying solar flux changes ionospheric temperatures and densities. Solar flux is the flow of energy and radiation arriving from the Sun. When it strengthens or fades across the solar cycle, the charged upper air, the ionosphere, answers.

The pair solve the flow and heat equations for electrons, ions, and neutral gases all at once. Their steady profiles for varied midday sun match observed data, they report. Neutral gas temperature and makeup, they find, dominate the charged particle patterns. Changes in atomic oxygen proved most effective at producing the observed trends in both the E and F regions.
nasa-tm-19710011600-phase-transitions-an:
John A Woollam and Paul R Aron of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a spring 1971 physics meeting in Cleveland. It studies a crystal with the formula CsMnCl3 2H2O. The crystal is an antiferromagnet, a material whose atomic magnets point in opposing patterns. The authors tracked how its length changed in magnetic fields.

They measured strain along all three crystal axes. Readings crossed the borders between the antiferromagnetic, spin flopped, and paramagnetic states. No earlier team had reported such length change data on a spin flopped antiferromagnet. The crystal cleaves into neat flat faces, which suited the fine measuring method used.
nasa-tm-19720010461-conversion-of-cardia:
Robert L Miller of the Lewis Research Center described this data conversion system in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2519. Heart performance records then lived as analog traces on paper and tape. Computers, though, need numbers in digital form. Miller's system reduced those traces and converted them directly. The results could enter a commercial time shared computer without hand typing. That saved hours of dull, error prone work.

Circuits in the system measure the analog blood pressure wave. They capture the peak and resting values of each heartbeat as they pass. Those systolic and diastolic readings are converted to digital form at once. Averaging circuits smooth the readings over several beats. The system bridged bedside instruments and digital analysis.
northern-trails-book-i:
William J. Long published Northern Trails, Book One, in 1905 at Stamford, Connecticut. It stands as book six of his Wood Folk series. A glossary of Indian names comes with the tales. Contents open with Wayeeses the Strong One and The Old Wolf's Challenge. Where the Trail Begins follows.

Noel and Mooka, The Way of the Wolf, and The White Wolf's Hunting fill the middle. Trails That Cross in the Snow closes the list. Picture captions speak of a great white wolf's terrible howl and a silent death watch. Long writes of wild animals as persons with lives of their own. Young readers of his day learned the woods through such tales.
podcast-dannyjones-U7niXhUEC-I:
Physicist Thomas Campbell worked for NASA and defense contractors before writing a trilogy arguing that reality is a computed simulation governed by consciousness. On Danny Jones's podcast, he explains why he left the inside track. He says he discovered the truth of the universe. In his account, the physical world is information, and love is its operating principle.

Campbell presents his theory with an engineer's diagrams and a mystic's conclusions, a combination that has earned him a devoted following. Jones works through the model and its tests. The theory is Campbell's own and stands outside physics as practiced, a fact he acknowledges cheerfully. The episode preserves a credentialed insider's complete alternative cosmology, delivered with unusual serenity. Listeners can take the physics as metaphor or as claim, which is the choice Campbell himself finally offers.
podcast-tuckercarlson-mUH4Co2wE-I:
Siblings Calley and Casey Means join Tucker Carlson to argue that Big Pharma profits by keeping people sick. Casey, a Stanford-trained surgeon, left medicine to co-found a health company with her brother Calley, a former industry lobbyist. Together they attack the system from inside knowledge.

The pair take on Ozempic, birth control pills, and the food and drug giants they say shape bad health policy. They argue that chronic disease is a business model, not an accident. Carlson asks what a real fix would look like. Health-conscious viewers get two whistleblowers naming names and numbers.
poems-1786-volume-i:
Helen Maria Williams published the first volume of her Poems in 1786, under the protection of the Queen, to whom the book is dedicated. Williams wrote the pieces young, with what her preface calls a confined education, and her first production was the legendary tale of Edwin and Eltruda, composed to pass solitary hours. Dr. Kippis encouraged her to print and offered to introduce the work to the world.

In her preface Williams explains herself with unusual frankness, asking pardon for faults of taste while trusting the poems' feeling. The dedication likewise refuses the usual flattery, claiming that praise poured freely from the heart suits a generous patron best. Volume one of two gives readers an early work by a writer who later became a noted witness of the French Revolution. Seen here at the very start of her career.
poems-by-jean-ingelow-in-two-volumes-vol:
Jean Ingelow's Poems appear in the author's complete edition, issued in Boston by Roberts Brothers in 1896, with this first volume of two. Ingelow dedicated the book to her brother George, dating the dedication from Kensington in June 1863, when her poetry first made her famous. She was among the most loved English poets of her century, especially for narrative verse and poems of home and faith.

Contents of the first volume open with Divided, then the two parts of Honors, followed by Requiescat in Pace, Supper at the Mill, Scholar and Carpenter, and the Star's Monument. Story poems sit beside lyrics of grief and devotion, the mixture that endeared Ingelow to Victorian readers on both sides of the Atlantic. The complete edition let her arrange the work of a lifetime as she wished it kept.
prue-and-i:
George William Curtis wrote a set of gentle sketches spoken by an old book-keeper whose whole world runs between his house and his office. His happiness rests in his wife Prue and their children, and he tells the reader so at the start.

The narrator finds romance without travel, seeing queens in an opera box and far countries in common days. He argues that a man need not roam to gain the charm of travel, since all lands and times repeat themselves in one small life. Readers get a beloved nineteenth-century portrait of contentment, humour, and married love.
queechy-volume-i: Queechy, volume one, is the Tauchnitz edition of the novel by Elizabeth Wetherell, the pen name of Susan Warner (1819-1885), whose Queechy first appeared in 1852. The pages here are the edition's title matter only. They name the Collection of British Authors, volume 311, dated 1854. The two-volume set is announced. The author's other Tauchnitz titles are listed too. They are The Wide Wide World and The Hills of the Shatemuc. Say and Seal and The Old Helmet follow.
representative-plays-by-american-dramati:
Love in '76, a short play billed as an incident of the Revolution, represents Oliver Bell Bunce in this set of American plays. Bunce lived from 1828 to 1890, and theatre histories seldom name him, the essay admits. Critics still praise this piece as parlour comedy, sprightly and fresh in invention.

It first played at Laura Keene's Theatre, New York, on February 28, 1857, for the Shirt Sewers' Union. Keene herself acted in it, on a double bill with Faust and Marguerite. Critics liked its lack of patriotic bombast and its smart social tone. Amateurs revived it in 1892 to fund a monument over the grave of Washington's mother.
sir-george-tressady-volume-i:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote this political novel in two volumes and inscribed it to her brother William Thomas Arnold. Ward had won fame with Marcella and Robert Elsmere. Volume one opens as a young man pulls his head in from a carriage window, glad some ordeal has ended.

Torches glare on a cheering crowd in the main street of Market Malford as the landau rolls away. Shops stand shut against the winter cold, and Lord Fontenoy warns that the bay mare may bolt. Election triumph and its costs drive Ward's study of a young member of Parliament and his world.
sketches-and-studies-in-italy-and-greece:
John Addington Symonds wrote these travel essays on Italy and Greece, gathered here across three volumes. Volume one opens with love of the Alps, winter nights at Davos, and old towns of Provence. Ajaccio, Como, Bergamo, and a Venetian medley follow among Lombard scenes.

Volume two turns to Ravenna, Rimini, Umbria in May, and the palace of Urbino, plus Florence and the Medici. Tuscan songs and Renaissance verse close that book. The third adds Siena, Monte Oliveto, and Montepulciano. Symonds blends landscape, art, and buried history in the rich, learned manner that made him Victorian England's great guide to Italy.
spenser-s-the-faerie-queene-book-i: George Armstrong Wauchope, who held the chair of English in the South Carolina College, edited Spenser's The Faerie Queene, Book I, with a first note and notes. Macmillan printed the book at New York and London in 1921, set up and first published in September 1903. The contents list a study in four heads: the age that made the poem, its author, a study of the poem itself, and a table of events in order of time.
studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-volume-:
Volume IV of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, dated 1927, treats Sexual Selection in Man under four heads: touch, smell, hearing, and vision. Ellis's preface warns that the work is tentative and preliminary, mapping a field in broad outline rather than reporting settled results.

He takes up Darwin's doctrine from The Descent of Man. He faults it on one point. Darwin mixed up the sensory stimuli that stir attraction with fine aesthetic choice. That confusion, Ellis says, misled many followers. The volume gathers facts on how each sense draws the sexes together, pointing where later, more exact study would likely find firmer ground. Ellis treats the senses as the true gateways of desire.
t-mann-bashan-and-i:
Thomas Mann's hunting pointer Bashan inspired the most personal book he ever wrote. Bashan and I, in Herman George Scheffauer's English translation, follows the dog through Munich fields and seasons while his master watches, thinks, and delights. Part memoir and part meditation, the little book charmed readers who knew Mann only as a solemn novelist.

Through Bashan, Mann reflects on nature, loyalty, patience, and the writer's odd working life. The dog's illnesses, hunts, and daily habits receive the same care Mann gave his fictional dynasties. Tender and funny, the portrait keeps breaking into unexpected depth. It shows a great ironist relaxing into plain affection. Animal lovers and Mann readers alike claim the book as a favorite.
the-ancient-banner-or-brief-sketches-of-:
Printed at Philadelphia by Joseph Kite and Company in 1846, The Ancient Banner offers brief sketches of persons and scenes in the early history of Friends, the Quakers. Its title page takes a motto from the sixtieth Psalm: a banner given to those who fear God, to be shown for the truth's sake.

The opening pages turn to verse. A poem tells how the Redeemer left his Father's bosom and took a servant's form, though he had reigned as a king before the words let there be light were spoken. It goes on to praise wonders worked in flesh: sickness fleeing at his word and the dead rising from the grave or the passing bier.
the-autobiography-of-a-journalist-volume:
William James Stillman published the first of two volumes of his life story in 1901. Early chapters recall a New England mother, nature worship, schooling, and college. He then turns to art study in America and England, a mission for Kossuth, and study in Paris.

Later headings in this volume cover spiritism, life in the wilderness, and the start of his work in journalism. Stillman writes about Cambridge, the Adirondack Club with Emerson and Agassiz, and time with Lowell. The contents close with the Adirondacks and Florida, joining art, travel, and reporting in one early career.
the-child-at-home-the-principles-of-fili:
John S. C. Abbott, author of The Mother at Home, wrote this guide for children on duty toward parents. The American Tract Society published it in New York, with rights entered in 1833 by Crocker and Brewster. Its title promises the principles of filial duty, shown in a familiar way.

Abbott's preface says the book was made for children in the families his earlier work had reached. He hopes it will stir gratitude for a parent's love and form characters fit for future usefulness and happiness. Solid instruction, not mere entertainment, is the stated aim, though he tries to dress it in an attractive form. He also asks that the child read it with a parent present, so the parent can seize the moment to apply its lessons. The book thus works as a shared family exercise, not a private pastime.
the-colloquies-of-erasmus-volume-i:
Erasmus's colloquies, his lively Latin dialogues, appear here in a translation by N. Bailey, edited with notes by the Rev. E. Johnson, M.A. Volume I was published in London in 1878. A life of Erasmus stands near the front, after Bailey's own title and preface and an admonitory note to the divines of Louvain.

The contents list dialogues on daily life and sharp practice alike. Courtesy in saluting and family discourse sit beside rash vows, benefice hunters, and a soldier's life. School pieces include the schoolmaster's admonitions, scholastic studies, and the child's piety. Other talks treat the profane feast and the religious treat, a lover and a maiden, the penitent virgin, and the uneasy wife. The shipwreck, the Franciscans as rich beggars, and the abbot and learned woman close the range. Bailey's version keeps Erasmus's mix of humor, teaching, and satire on folly.
the-dawn-and-the-day-or-the-buddha-and-t:
Henry T. Niles published The Dawn and the Day, or The Buddha and the Christ, Part I, at Toledo, Ohio, in 1894 through the Blade Printing and Paper Company. His preface opens with Humboldt on the Andes. He found Alpine plants there and read the cause in his barometer and the rocks around him: a case of laws of order and universal harmony.

Niles turns to Max Mueller, who found the most ancient Hindoos worshipping Dyaus Pitar, the same name as the Greek Zeus Pater and the Roman Jupiter. Rather than guess at beliefs carried across seas, Niles sees the shared name as the human soul's common yearning for a loving Father. He faults missionaries who, finding core truths of their own faith in Buddha's teachings, strained to prove those truths borrowed from early Christians in the East.
the-decameron-volume-i: Only a Project Gutenberg header stands at the head of this record for The Decameron, Volume I, by Giovanni Boccaccio, in J. M. Rigg's translation. The header dates the electronic text to February 2003, numbers it Etext 3726, and names Donna Holsten as its producer, with the usual notes on copyright and keeping the file. No contents, prologue, or tale text follows in what is present here.
the-dramatic-works-of-gerhart-hauptmann-:
Volume one of The Dramatic Works of Gerhart Hauptmann, in a 1912 authorized edition edited by Ludwig Lewisohn, holds social dramas. Its contents name Before Dawn, The Weavers, The Beaver Coat, and The Conflagration. Lewisohn took the first, third, and fourth plays into English himself, while Mary Morison rendered The Weavers.

A life of Hauptmann opens the volume. Born in a Silesian village in 1862, he sprang from inn-keeping folk whose roots touched the weavers' hard fate. His plays give the poor weight and grief on stage. The set marks his Nobel-year fame.
the-future-of-the-colored-race-in-americ: Only the old Project Gutenberg header is present here, before the book itself begins. It names The Future of the Colored Race in America by William Aikman, and gives the book's release data. No title page, contents list, or page of the article can be read in what is present, so nothing about the author's argument can be described from the front matter alone.
the-garden-you-and-i: Barbara, author of The Garden of a Commuter's Wife and People of the Whirlpool, wrote The Garden, You, and I, printed at New York in 1906. Only the front matter is present here: the title pages and a dedication to three sets of initials. A seaside garden is named as the front picture. No chapter text is included in this portion, so the talks on gardens and home life inside cannot be stated from this front matter alone.
the-glands-regulating-personality-a-stud:
Louis Berman wrote The Glands Regulating Personality. He was a doctor and an associate in biological chemistry at Columbia University. The book is dated 1922. Its full title calls it a study of the glands of internal secretion. It links those glands to the types of human nature. A quote from Francis Bacon's Novum Organum of 1620 stands at the front.

The contents run from how the glands were found. They cover the thyroid, the pituitary, and the adrenal glands. They cover the gonads and the thymus. Later chapters ask how glands shape the body, sex, and the mind. They sort people into types of personality. They test the scheme on historic figures. They end with uses and effects on human evolution. Berman opens by noting that each person studies human nature all his life.
the-grounds-of-an-opinion-on-the-policy-:
Rev. T. R. Malthus wrote The Grounds of an Opinion on the Policy of Restricting the Importation of Foreign Corn. Malthus taught history and political economy at the East India College in Hertfordshire. John Murray printed the pamphlet in London in 1815. It is meant as an appendix to his Observations on the Corn Laws of 1814. In those Observations, he says, he stated both sides with strict impartiality. He gave no decided opinion of his own.

That restraint, he now argues, had a purpose. The public had to be prepared for the consequences of the decision, on whichever side it fell. The statements having been given, he now speaks freely. He now gives his own view plainly, with no stake of his own in the matter: a settled judgment, reached on purpose. He comes down for keeping some check on foreign corn coming in.
the-jungle-fugitives-a-tale-of-life-and-:
Edward S. Ellis published this story collection in 1903. Hurst and Company of New York issued it. A tale of life and adventure in India leads it. Many stories of American daring follow. The contents promise boys lost in the woods. Boys lost in the South Sea appear too. A battle in the air, cyclones, and a blizzard come next. A waterspout, a heroic woman, and a writing in a bottle follow. A fool of a genius closes the list.

The title story opens in the spring of 1857. All through India, Ellis writes, rumblings had been heard for months. The coming uprising spread and took root. India's population was five times England's then. His jungle fugitives belong to the Indian Mutiny. American boys' fiction imagined that revolt as flight and pursuit. The country stands on the edge of revolt throughout.
the-life-and-letters-of-walter-h-page-vo:
Burton J. Hendrick wrote the life and letters of Walter H. Page, ambassador to Britain during the First World War. Volume one appeared at Garden City, New York, in 1922. His prefatory note thanks embassy secretary Irwin Laughlin for reading the manuscript and adding corrections.

Hendrick also drew on long talks with Viscount Grey and on Foreign Office papers covering Page work from 1913 to 1916. Page letters show an American envoy caught between neutral orders from Washington and sympathy for Britain. Readers get diplomacy told through private writing rather than official reports alone.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-01: Motley's first PG volume is dated 1855. It carries an editor's note on the author. The same note opens the complete records in the set. It sketches his Dorchester birth in 1814. It names his early novels for readers. It lists his ministries in Austria and in England. Holmes is quoted on European sympathy there. Free institutions win that sympathy, Holmes argued in 1863. Only the volume heading is present on these pages. The opening of that note appears with it. The historical introduction itself does not appear.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-10:
Motley's tenth volume treats the year 1566. Chapter six begins with Francis Junius preaching. He preaches at Culemburg House to the confederates. The Compromise forms in those meetings of nobles. Portraits of Sainte Aldegonde sketch the signers' leaders. Louis of Nassau stands among those portraits in the summary. Orange keeps spies over Philip's court during the crisis.

The people despair and emigrate to England in numbers. A Request is prepared at Breda and Hoogstraaten meetings. Petitioners arrive in Brussels with the document at last. Margaret shows emotion at its presentation to her. Brederode speaks for the confederates in the audience. Berlaymont's memorable sarcasm enters the summary at that moment. Petition politics carries this first half of the year.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-12:
Motley's record for 1567 part one carries a clash. Its own pages head it as volume thirteen. The record title calls it volume twelve instead. Readers should note that numbering clash at the start. Its summary lists Calvinist defeats at Lannoy first. Government elation and cruelties against country people follow. Courage among the inhabitants answers those cruelties.

Noircarmes wakes early in January of 1567. He falls on a locksmith's small army at once. Brederode levies troops at Antwerp in response. Orange refuses a new oath demanded by government. He offers his resignation of all offices instead. Three days of tumult shake Antwerp afterward. Orange suppresses them by wisdom and by courage. Defeat and discipline close the year's opening movement.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-14:
Headed volume fifteen in its own pages, though the record calls it volume fourteen, this portion covers 1568 in chapter two. Orange, Louis, and Hoogstraaten are cited before the Blood Council, Orange answers by letter, and his son is seized, while a death sentence against the whole Netherlands population is proclaimed.

Egmont and Horn face interrogatories in prison as their countesses, knights of the Fleece, and the Emperor plead in vain against Alva and Philip. Obsequious Viglius helps set aside the Fleece statutes. Legal forms are kept while mercy is refused, which is Motley's point.
the-river-and-i: John G. Neihardt's river book appears in a new Macmillan edition at New York in 1927, reissued in new format that October from a copyright of 1910 and dedicated to his mother. Companion titles listed include Indian tales, poetic studies, a quest, and songs of Hugh Glass, Indian wars, and three friends. Here only those lists, title pages, and dedication are present, so the river narrative itself does not appear.
the-slave-trade-domestic-and-foreign-why:
H. C. Carey wrote The Slave Trade, Domestic and Foreign, asking why it exists and how it may be extinguished. Carey also wrote Principles of Political Economy, his title page notes.
